results.flow_summary: Reserve-missed outcome. The Chainlink wrapper callback resolves the raffle to CashWon because totalEntries is below the sponsor-chosen reserveEntries. After that, any account can call releaseSponsorPrize() with no arguments. The guarded handler accepts CashWon and requires prizeClaimed == false. It caches the immutable sponsorRecipient and sets prizeClaimed = true. It then calls the sponsor-chosen prizeToken.transferFrom(raffle, sponsorRecipient, prizeTokenId), checks that prizeToken.ownerOf(prizeTokenId) == sponsorRecipient, and emits SponsorPrizeReleased. The flow ends with the NFT out of escrow. It does not depend on settleWinningTicket, the winner's cash redemption or releaseSponsorProceeds, which can happen before or after it.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The caller sends no calldata. It controls only the trigger and its timing: any block after CashWon, before or after settlement or the winner's cash redemption. At the sink, the target is the stored prizeToken, from is address(this), to is the stored sponsorRecipient and the token ID is the stored prizeTokenId. The sponsor fixed all of these in createRaffle. The CashWon result itself comes from buyer totalEntries compared with the sponsor's reserveEntries, plus VRF randomness.
results.flow_terminal_action: ERC-721 transferFrom of the escrowed prize from the raffle clone to sponsorRecipient. prizeClaimed becomes permanently true and SponsorPrizeReleased is emitted.
results.flow_security_relevance: At Raffle.sol:404 the escrowed NFT leaves the raffle in the reserve-missed result, while the winning ticket is owed 80% cash. Any account can force this transfer. Its correctness depends on CashWon never being reachable when the reserve was met. It also depends on the sponsor-chosen, untrusted prize contract being called only after the prizeClaimed latch is set.

results.flow_summary: Refund outcome. enableRefunds moves the clone to Refunding by one of three routes: the sponsor closes an empty raffle at any time (or anyone does from endTime), a sold raffle gets no draw request by endTime+2 days, or a Drawing raffle's callback misses drawRequestedAt+2 days. After that, any account can call releaseSponsorPrize(). The handler accepts Refunding, requires prizeClaimed == false and sets it. It then transfers the NFT to sponsorRecipient through the untrusted prize contract, checks ownerOf and emits SponsorPrizeReleased. Ticket holders separately burn their tickets for 100% refunds via refundTickets. The prize release does not touch refund liability.
results.flow_input_to_sink: No calldata. The actor controls only when the call lands relative to the enableRefunds transition. Indirectly, the route matters: sponsor early close of an empty raffle, a missed draw-request window, or a missed VRF callback window. The sink arguments are the stored, sponsor-chosen prizeToken, prizeTokenId and sponsorRecipient.
results.flow_terminal_action: ERC-721 transferFrom returns the escrowed prize to sponsorRecipient in the Refunding outcome. prizeClaimed becomes true and SponsorPrizeReleased is emitted.
results.flow_security_relevance: Raffle.sol:404 returns the prize whenever the raffle is Refunding. This is safe only if Refunding is terminal and cannot coexist with a VRF resolution: callbacks must land strictly before drawRequestedAt+2 days, and refunds open only at or after it. results.flow_summary: While Raffle.sol:404 runs, control passes to the sponsor-chosen prize contract, with the raffle as msg.sender and prizeClaimed already true. Re-entering any nonReentrant raffle function reverts with ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall. That covers releaseSponsorPrize, settleWinningTicket, redeemWinningTicket, refundTickets, releaseSponsorProceeds, releaseProtocolFees, enableRefunds, buyEntries and requestDraw. The unguarded surface stays reachable: (1) the ticket ERC-721 functions approve, setApprovalForAll, transferFrom and safeTransferFrom, through the _update override, which screens destinations with factory calls and rejects the prize token as a ticket owner; (2) onERC721Received, which rejects unless status is AwaitingPrize; (3) receive, which reverts; (4) rawFulfillRandomWords, wrapper-only; (5) initialize, which reverts AlreadyInitialized; (6) all views, which show prizeClaimed = true mid-transfer. Other clones and the factory have their own guards and can be called. The follow-up ownerOf call is a STATICCALL, so the prize contract can only return an arbitrary owner, revert or burn gas. If its transferFrom does nothing, or moves the token elsewhere, while ownerOf returns sponsorRecipient, the raffle finalizes the release without a real transfer.

results.flow_terminal_action: One of two outcomes. Either the whole call reverts (a re-entry or other failure bubbles up), or the release is finalized (prizeClaimed = true, SponsorPrizeReleased emitted) and the actual asset movement is whatever the prize contract implemented.
results.flow_security_relevance: Raffle.sol:404 is an untrusted external call made after a state write, with the raffle as caller. Containment depends on every value-moving function sharing the per-clone nonReentrant guard, while the ticket ERC-721 surface and views remain open. The delivery check trusts the same untrusted contract.

results.flow_summary: sponsorRecipient is screened against protocol infrastructure (the factory, implementation, quote token, VRF wrapper, prize token and registered clones) only at creation, in RaffleFactory._validateCreateParams and in Raffle.initialize/_isProtocolDestination. Clones are deployed with CREATE, so future clone addresses can be predicted from the factory nonce. A not-yet-deployed address passes both checks because it has no code and is not registered. output_json.stub_explanation: No concrete, attacker-reachable vulnerability in the NftWon releaseProtocolFees flow. (1) protocolFees is written only by _settleWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:555), which is gated once by settlementComplete (L534/L551), and by releaseProtocolFees, which zeroes it (L388) inside nonReentrant before the USDC call, so the fee cannot be paid twice. (2) In the NftWon branch, fee = mulDiv(pot,500,10000) (exactly 50,000 units per 1 USDC entry, no dust) and sponsorProceeds = pot - fee (L544). Together they equal the escrowed USDC. Once NftWon is set, no other USDC outflow is reachable: refundTickets needs Refunding, enableRefunds needs Active/Drawing, NftWon redemption moves only the NFT, and releaseSponsorProceeds pays its own separately zeroed amount. So the fee cannot cut into the sponsor's 95%, and call order does not matter. (3) The destination is protocolTreasury: it is copied from the factory immutable at initialize (RaffleFactory.sol:114 to Raffle.sol:199) and never rewritten, so neither the caller nor the sponsor can change it. (4) The payout-time check _isProtocolDestination (L599-604) uses the same fixed inputs that passed at initialize. raffleImplementation() and isRaffle() are view getters on the immutable factory and cannot revert or be manipulated. isRaffle(treasury) can never become true: clones get new CREATE addresses, and a clone at the treasury's address would fail initialize on destination == address(this). So the release cannot be blocked or redirected. (5) Re-entry is not possible: canonical USDC has no recipient hooks, every state-changing entry point shares the nonReentrant guard, and an untrusted prize token's transferFrom runs while the guard is held. The clone's guard slot starts at 0, which is not ENTERED, and is reset after each call, so the lock never stays set. (6) The caller controls only msg.sender and timing. Front-running, limiting gas or repeating the call either reverts atomically or pays the same fixed amount to the same treasury.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable issue in the CashWon releaseProtocolFees flow. Raffle.sol:385-392 reads only protocolFees, reverts if it is zero, sets it to zero before the transfer, and pays the fixed protocolTreasury under the shared nonReentrant guard. It never reads or changes winnerProceeds or sponsorProceeds. protocolFees is set in only one place, _settleWinningTicket, and settlementComplete stops that from running twice (L534, L551). Gross is always N*1,000,000 USDC units, so the 5% fee is exactly N*50,000, the 80% winner share is exactly N*800,000, and the sponsor gets exactly N*150,000. These sum to unsettledPot with no rounding drift. CashWon is final: enableRefunds only accepts Active or Drawing, and the VRF callback only accepts Drawing. So no refund liability can coexist with these three cash claims. USDC leaves the clone only through redeemWinningTicket, refundTickets, releaseSponsorProceeds and releaseProtocolFees, and each pays out only its own bucket, so the balance always covers the remaining claims in any order. The treasury is the factory's immutable address, checked against protocol addresses at initialize (L190), and those checks cannot change later, so fees cannot get stuck. The pinned OpenZeppelin and Chainlink files match dependency-hashes.json. Releasing the fee before the winner redeems is intended: the spec says the sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement. The caller controls only timing and msg.sender, and neither lets them move funds away from the winner or the sponsor.

L555 in _settleWinningTicket runs only when settlementComplete is false (L534) and status is NftWon or CashWon (L536), and it sets settlementComplete=true (L551). L388 zeroes the fee before the transfer. A clone can therefore be allocated a fee at most once, and a released fee can never be allocated again. (2) Status changes only move forward. NftWon/CashWon can be entered only from Drawing, through the callback that the wrapper authenticates (rawFulfillRandomWords checks msg.sender, L509-521). Refunding can be entered only from Active or Drawing (L279-294). So the refund outcome never gets a fee, and a settled clone can never enter Refunding. enableRefunds moves the entire unsettledPot into remainingRefundLiability. (3) The constructor locks the implementation (initialized=true, status Refunding). A clone not created by the factory cannot pass initialize (L178 OnlyFactory). It stays in AwaitingPrize with prizeToken=0, so onERC721Received can never activate it, and its fee storage stays zero. (4) The release follows checks-effects-interactions: the fee is zeroed before the transfer. Every state-changing entry point is nonReentrant, and the OZ 5.6.1 guard keeps its flag in a namespaced storage slot. Clones are deployed with CREATE and start with zeroed storage. The only inline assembly is the native-fee refund call in requestDraw, so no storage write can bypass these checks. (5) protocolTreasury is the factory's immutable treasury. It is checked with _isProtocolDestination at initialization against the same stored prizeToken that is checked again at release. The only term that can change, isRaffle(treasury), cannot become true, so a sponsor cannot pick a prize token that later locks the fees. (6) The revert path changes no state and makes no external call. A successful call always pays the fixed treasury exactly its allocated 5% (at least 50,000 units, since grossPot >= 1e6). Anyone can call settleWinningTicket, so fees cannot be stuck forever. Calling at a chosen time gives an attacker nothing: they cannot redirect the funds, repeat the payout, or draw from balances that back winner, sponsor, or refund liabilities.

output_json.stub_explanation: This flow has no vulnerability that an attacker can trigger. releaseProtocolFees (Raffle.sol:385-392) reads protocolFees, sets it to zero, then pays it through _transferQuote (L564-567). That always sends the full amount to protocolTreasury. The treasury is written once in the factory's initialize, comes from RaffleFactory's immutable protocolTreasury (Factory L87 → Raffle L199), and nothing else can change it, so a caller cannot redirect or split the payout. SafeERC20.safeTransfer uses bubble=true, so any failed USDC call or false return reverts the whole transaction. That revert also undoes protocolFees = 0 and the reentrancy-guard write. Nothing is lost, and there is no one-time flag or partial state for a caller to waste or race. The only failure causes named for this flow are USDC being paused, or the treasury or clone being blacklisted. The treasury address check also cannot be turned against the payout. output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable issue in this flow. The pot unsettledPot only grows in buyEntries, by entryCount × 1,000,000, and only buyEntries brings USDC in. Until settlement, the only payout is refundTickets, and that needs Refunding status, which can never coexist with CashWon or NftWon. In _settleWinningTicket (L539-555), the protocol fee is floor(g·500/10000) and the cash prize is floor(g·8000/10000). Their sum is at most 0.85·g, so the sponsor amount g − fee − cash at L547 can never underflow. The three amounts add up to exactly g. Because g is always a multiple of 1e6, the split is exactly 50,000 / 800,000 / 150,000 units per entry with no rounding, and any rounding would go to the sponsor as the remainder. A Python check over a wide range of g and the uint128 edge values found no violations. Settlement runs only once (settlementComplete check at L534). Status cannot go back from CashWon/NftWon to Refunding, because enableRefunds only works from Active or Drawing. fulfillRandomWords needs Drawing status and can only be called by the wrapper. releaseSponsorProceeds (L375-382) reads only its own sponsorProceeds slot, zeroes it before the transfer, and is nonReentrant. It never touches winnerProceeds or protocolFees, and the contract's USDC balance always covers the sum of all accounted slots. So the three payouts can run in any order without draining each other. The caller has no input and cannot change the recipient (sponsorRecipient). Whether the recipient is a protocol destination at L565 depends only on the sponsor's own choice of address, so a third party cannot trigger that revert. Any harm from a bad choice falls on the sponsor alone.

output_json.stub_explanation: No supported vulnerability in Raffle.releaseSponsorProceeds (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:375-382). A search of src/ shows sponsorProceeds is written in only two places. The first is _settleWinningTicket at L554. That write runs at most once (L534 settlementComplete), only when status is NftWon or CashWon (L536), and only for a ticket whose stored range contains winningEntry (winningEntry >= 1 and unminted IDs have range 0..0). The second is the zeroing at L378, which happens before the external call (checks-effects-interactions, plus nonReentrant). The zero check at L377 therefore blocks a payout in every case named in the flow. (1) Before settlement: Active and Drawing raffles cannot settle, and NftWon or CashWon raffles keep sponsorProceeds at 0 until someone settles them. (2) Refunding: enableRefunds (L276-300) can only leave Active or Drawing, and it only moves unsettledPot into remainingRefundLiability. fulfillRandomWords needs status Drawing and block.timestamp < callbackDeadline, while enableRefunds from Drawing needs block.timestamp >= callbackDeadline. So a raffle cannot be both resolved and refunding, and the refund branch can never get a nonzero sponsorProceeds. (3) Locked implementation: the constructor sets status Refunding and initialized=true, initialize is blocked, and onERC721Received needs AwaitingPrize, so sponsorProceeds stays 0. A clone deployed outside the factory cannot be initialized (OnlyFactory) and also has sponsorProceeds 0. (4) Repeat calls: the first release zeroes the value and settlement cannot run again. When the value is nonzero, the amount is backed: the protocol fee, winner share and sponsor remainder add up exactly to grossPot (unsettledPot, which buyEntries funds 1:1 and nothing changes after Active ends). The release pays only the stored sponsorRecipient, which only initialize sets. Under OpenZeppelin 5.6.1, ReentrancyGuard keeps its flag in a namespaced storage slot. Fresh clones read that slot as 0, not ENTERED, so the guard works on clones. Letting anyone trigger the release is intended: the caller has no input and cannot redirect or inflate the payout.

output_json.stub_explanation:
The proposed lock is real but self-inflicted, so it is not a vulnerability that an outside actor can exploit. Only the sponsor sets sponsorRecipient: RaffleFactory.createRaffle (L97-121) passes params.sponsorRecipient, with sponsor = msg.sender, and Raffle.initialize (L193-198) stores it. No other account can change it later.

For releaseSponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:375) to hit InvalidQuoteDestination at _transferQuote (L565), sponsorRecipient must be the address of a future factory clone. Clones.clone uses CREATE (Clones.sol:57), so that address is keccak256(rlp(factory, nonce)). Nobody holds a private key for it.

A third party cannot make a victim's recipient collide with that address:
- An EOA would need a 160-bit preimage match against the factory's sequential nonce addresses, which is infeasible. An attacker can only advance the nonce one full createRaffle (with an escrowed NFT) at a time.
- An address that already had code at creation can never be CREATEd into.
- A counterfactual CREATE2 wallet faces the same infeasible collision.

So the case only arises if the sponsor deliberately picks a future clone address. No tooling in the repo does this: the package has only src and config, with no scripts or frontend.

The loss also exists without the L602-603 check. If release ran before the clone was deployed, the USDC would go to an address with no key. Once the address becomes a clone, it has no rescue or withdrawal path for untracked USDC; accounting is state-based (accountedQuoteBalance, L468-470). The check therefore causes no loss that wouldn't otherwise occur. It just enforces the design rule "Never move assets between raffle clones." The result is equivalent to the sponsor choosing a burn address.

Only the sponsor's own proceeds are affected:
- Winner redemption (L339-342) pays the ticket owner.
- Refunds (L369) pay msg.sender.
- Protocol fees (L385-391) go to the immutable treasury.
None of these depend on sponsorRecipient.

isRaffle is never cleared and Raffle clones cannot self-destruct, so the classification can only become stricter over time. No external actor gains anything or harms another user.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability that an external actor can exploit was found in this flow. releaseSponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:375) takes no input and is nonReentrant. It zeroes sponsorProceeds before calling _transferQuote, which first calls the factory's view-only screening functions (raffleImplementation and isRaffle, via staticcall) and then calls SafeERC20.safeTransfer on the canonical USDC. USDC has no transfer hooks. The payout always goes to sponsorRecipient, which the sponsor chose and which was screened when the raffle was created (RaffleFactory.sol:163-168, Raffle.sol:193-198). A caller can therefore only choose when the sponsor gets paid; they cannot change the recipient or the amount. Paying out twice is not possible because the balance is zeroed first and the function is nonReentrant. The revert described in the lead happens only when USDC's own pause or blacklist controls refuse the transfer. Those controls belong to Circle, and DESIGN.md names the quote token as a trusted canonical dependency. No caller can trigger a pause or blacklist through this contract. If the transfer reverts, the whole transaction rolls back, so sponsorProceeds and accountedQuoteBalance stay consistent and the release can be retried once the restriction is lifted. No funds are lost or redirected. Sponsor proceeds are tracked and released separately from settlement, winner redemption (redeemWinningTicket), treasury fees (releaseProtocolFees) and refunds (refundTickets), so a recipient that cannot be paid does not block anyone else. There is no rescue path and the recipient is immutable; this matches the documented design of no administrator, mutable configuration or upgrade. The resulting dependency on USDC's availability is an accepted trust assumption and cannot be triggered by the stated actor.

(2) The call into the untrusted prize contract is protected. The function is nonReentrant: a clone's guard slot starts at 0, which is not ENTERED, so the first call passes. prizeClaimed is set to true before prizeToken.transferFrom and is never reset. The recipient is the sponsorRecipient fixed at initialization, the token ID is the stored prizeTokenId, and ownerOf is a STATICCALL checked afterwards. During the transfer, every function that moves value (buy, draw, refund, settle, redeem, releases) is nonReentrant. onERC721Received needs AwaitingPrize, and rawFulfillRandomWords only accepts the VRF wrapper. output_json.stub_explanation: The status check at Raffle.sol:397 holds; I found no way around it. Only six places in the code write `status`. (1) The constructor sets Refunding, but only on the locked implementation. There `prizeToken` is address(0), so the call to `transferFrom` reverts on the extcodesize check. (2) `initialize` sets AwaitingPrize, and only the factory can call it. (3) `onERC721Received` moves AwaitingPrize to Active. (4) `requestDraw` moves Active to Drawing. (5) `enableRefunds` moves Active or Drawing to Refunding. (6) `fulfillRandomWords` moves Drawing to NftWon or CashWon. NftWon, CashWon and Refunding are final: no function moves a raffle out of them. So the NFT cannot be released in CashWon or Refunding and then become owed to a winner. An NftWon raffle can also never move into a state where release is allowed. The timing checks do not overlap. `requestDraw` needs time before the draw deadline (Raffle.sol:245). `enableRefunds` with entries sold needs time at or after that deadline (Raffle.sol:287). The VRF callback is ignored at or after the callback deadline (Raffle.sol:512), and `enableRefunds` from Drawing needs that same deadline to have passed (Raffle.sol:291). The sponsor's immediate refund switch only works while `totalEntries == 0`; after one purchase the deadline branch applies. `prizeClaimed` is set before the external call, and the function is `nonReentrant`. The only other path that transfers the prize is `redeemWinningTicket`, which runs only in NftWon. While the untrusted prize contract runs inside `transferFrom` or `ownerOf`, the only Raffle functions it can enter are the unguarded ticket ERC-721 functions, view functions, and `onERC721Received`. `onERC721Received` reverts outside AwaitingPrize. A sponsor-controlled contract could push a new clone to Refunding and release the prize during `createRaffle`. If it does, the factory's Active check at RaffleFactory.sol:132 reverts the whole creation. The caller supplies no parameters; only call timing varies, and every non-terminal or NftWon timing reverts before any state change.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability found. The replay latch at packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:400 works as intended, and no external actor can bypass it or turn it against anyone else. (1) prizeClaimed is set to true in only two places, never reset, and the two writers can never both run. Line 403 (releaseSponsorPrize) runs only under CashWon or Refunding. Line 331 (redeemWinningTicket) runs only under NftWon. (2) CashWon, Refunding and NftWon are terminal states. Status is written only at lines 205, 252, 299, 428 and 521. Each of those writes needs AwaitingPrize, Active or Drawing as the starting state. fulfillRandomWords can only be called by the trusted VRF wrapper (VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.rawFulfillRandomWords), so a raffle can never leave CashWon or Refunding, or move into NftWon, after a release. (3) The latch is set before the untrusted prizeToken.transferFrom and ownerOf calls, and the function is nonReentrant. OpenZeppelin 5.x ReentrancyGuard keeps its flag in a namespaced storage slot that starts at 0 in clones and still blocks reentry. A malicious prize contract therefore cannot re-enter releaseSponsorPrize or any other nonReentrant function that moves USDC or the prize. The ticket ERC721 functions and onERC721Received remain callable without the guard, but they give it nothing: onERC721Received requires AwaitingPrize. (4) The ownerOf check at line 405 undoes everything, including prizeClaimed, when delivery fails. With an honest token, the latch cannot end up set while the NFT stays in escrow. A malicious prize contract can only fake delivery of the sponsor's own fake asset. (5) On the implementation contract (status Refunding, prizeToken = address(0)) the call reverts on the call to an address with no code. Unregistered third-party clones stay in AwaitingPrize and fail the status gate. (6) Two leftover concerns are not attacks: an NFT pushed back with a plain transferFrom is unrecoverable, and releaseSponsorPrize does not re-check whether sponsorRecipient is a raffle clone. The first is documented design that needs the NFT owner's own action (lines 409-411). The second can only be caused by a sponsor deliberately setting sponsorRecipient to a future clone address, and it only harms that sponsor. The only input a caller controls is when they call. Calling earlier or later just delivers the prize to the fixed sponsorRecipient, or reverts.

output_json.stub_explanation: Nobody other than the sponsor can make releaseSponsorPrize fail permanently, and when it does fail only the sponsor's own NFT is affected. (1) It uses plain IERC721.transferFrom (Raffle.sol:404), which never calls back into sponsorRecipient, so the recipient cannot block delivery. (2) The raffle is the token owner and exposes no approve function for the prize token, so for a standard ERC-721 (OZ 5.x transferFrom) no other account can take the token or make the transfer revert. (3) If a caller supplies too little gas or the prize contract reverts, the high-level call bubbles up the error. The whole transaction reverts, the prizeClaimed latch set at line 403 is rolled back, and anyone can call again. Nothing is left half-updated. (4) The function is nonReentrant, and so is every other state-changing path in Raffle. That leaves a reentering prize contract only ticket ERC-721 transfers and view calls, which cannot affect this flow. (5) A permanent refusal (paused, soulbound or blocklisted token, a lying ownerOf, a self-destructed contract) can only come from the prize contract and sponsorRecipient that the sponsor chose at createRaffle. That is self-harm to the sponsor's own NFT. (6) No third party's funds depend on this call. Refunds (refundTickets), the cash-winner payout (redeemWinningTicket, CashWon branch), sponsor proceeds and protocol fees never call the prize contract; _transferQuote only compares addresses against prizeToken. So a refusing prize contract cannot lock ticket holders', the winner's or the treasury's USDC. (7) The missing rescue or alternate-recipient path is a documented design choice. Raffle.sol:24-25 says 'no administrator or rescue path', and IRaffle.sol:14-15 says 'Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s'. Reverting every effect when delivery fails is exactly what DESIGN.md requires.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in Raffle.releaseSponsorPrize (Raffle.sol:395-407). (1) Re-entry is contained. The function is nonReentrant. In a clone the OpenZeppelin guard slot starts at 0, gets set to ENTERED and then reset, so the guard works without a constructor. prizeClaimed is set before the external call, and a revert at any point undoes it. Every function that moves value, settles or changes status is nonReentrant: buyEntries, requestDraw, enableRefunds, settleWinningTicket, redeemWinningTicket, refundTickets, releaseSponsorProceeds, releaseProtocolFees and releaseSponsorPrize. The unguarded functions give the prize contract no special rights. Ticket approve/transferFrom need the caller to own the ticket or be approved for it, and _update refuses to make the prize token a ticket owner. The raffle itself never owns tickets or grants approvals. onERC721Received needs status AwaitingPrize, initialize reverts with AlreadyInitialized, rawFulfillRandomWords accepts only the wrapper, and receive reverts. The raffle never approves USDC to anyone, so code running as the raffle's callee cannot take the pot. Calls into other clones or factory.createRaffle are things any account can already do. (2) CashWon and Refunding are terminal. fulfillRandomWords ignores callbacks unless status is Drawing, and enableRefunds only starts from Active or Drawing. The release can therefore never take the NFT from an NftWon winner. In CashWon, prizeClaimed is not used by the cash branch of redeemWinningTicket, and the release does not touch winnerProceeds, sponsorProceeds, protocolFees or refund liability. (3) The ownerOf delivery check does trust the prize contract. A lying contract can finalize the release without a real transfer, but the only party hurt is the sponsorRecipient. That address was chosen by the sponsor, who also chose and deposited the prize contract. A prize contract that lies here could also have faked the deposit, so no third party (ticket holders, cash winner, treasury) loses anything. Ticket transfers and USDC payouts never call the prize contract, so a malicious prize cannot block refunds or cash claims. (4) Unlike _transferQuote, the release does not re-check sponsorRecipient against _isProtocolDestination. The only way that address can later become a protocol address is if the sponsor deliberately sets it to a predicted future factory CREATE address. That harms only the sponsor's own NFT, and no outside attacker can cause it.

output_json.stub_explanation: The mechanics are real, but the only person who can set this up is the sponsor, and the only thing lost is the sponsor's own NFT. (1) How it works: a not-yet-deployed address predicted from the factory's CREATE nonce passes the creation checks. In RaffleFactory.sol:166, isRaffle is false for it. In Raffle.sol:602, the registry lookup is skipped because the address has no code. releaseSponsorPrize then sends the NFT with a plain transferFrom and does not re-check the destination (Raffle.sol:402-405). (2) Only the sponsor controls the destination. sponsorRecipient comes from the createRaffle caller's own params (RaffleFactory.sol:112-113) and never changes. The NFT must be the sponsor's own, because the factory pulls it with safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, ...) at RaffleFactory.sol:128. The release only runs in CashWon or Refunding (Raffle.sol:397), when the NFT is going back to the sponsor anyway. Whoever calls releaseSponsorPrize has no inputs and cannot change the recipient or the token. A third party cannot turn an address the sponsor picked into a clone, because clone addresses are fixed by the factory address and its nonce. So the clone destination only happens if the sponsor deliberately chooses a future clone address. (3) The impact is self-inflicted and harms no one else. The sponsor loses their own returned NFT, which is the same as sending it to any clone or burn address themselves. Raffle.sol:409-411 already documents that NFTs pushed in with unsafe transferFrom stay outside accounting. The receiving clone is not affected: onERC721Received does not run, and its status, prizeToken/prizeTokenId, USDC accounting and ownerOf check on its own prize stay the same. The NFT cannot be double-claimed, because one token cannot be escrowed by two clones. Winners, ticket holders and the treasury are not affected, since redeem, refund and fee paths do not depend on sponsorRecipient. The related revert in releaseSponsorProceeds also only strands the sponsor's own proceeds. Reentrancy from the untrusted prize contract is blocked by nonReentrant on every state-changing function, and prizeClaimed is set before the external call. No other party can realistically exploit this flow.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability: calling releaseSponsorPrize() on the shared implementation always reverts and has no effect. The RaffleFactory constructor (RaffleFactory.sol:89) deploys the implementation, and its constructor (Raffle.sol:164-165) sets initialized = true and status = Refunding. It never writes prizeToken, prizeTokenId or sponsorRecipient, so those stay zero. Nothing can change them later. initialize() reverts with AlreadyInitialized (Raffle.sol:177). The other state-writing paths all fail on the implementation: buyEntries and requestDraw need Active, enableRefunds rejects Refunding, settle and redeem need NftWon or CashWon, refundTickets needs tickets and none can be minted, and onERC721Received needs AwaitingPrize. On a direct call, the guard passes because the constructor set the slot to NOT_ENTERED, the Refunding status passes the gate at Raffle.sol:397, and prizeClaimed is false (Raffle.sol:400). Then IERC721(address(0)).transferFrom(...) runs at Raffle.sol:404. IERC721.transferFrom returns nothing, so Solidity keeps its code-existence check, and address(0) has no code on Ethereum or Sepolia. The call reverts and undoes the prizeClaimed = true write at Raffle.sol:403. Even without that check, ownerOf at Raffle.sol:405 expects a returned address, and ABI decoding empty return data would revert anyway. The implementation also cannot hold a real prize. Its onERC721Received rejects safe transfers because the status is not AwaitingPrize. Its prizeToken is zero and cannot be set, so this function has no way to reach an NFT pushed in with unsafe transferFrom. The implementation has no delegatecall or selfdestruct, so clones are unaffected. On real clones the function is also safe. It sets prizeClaimed before the external call and is nonReentrant. CashWon and Refunding are terminal states that cannot overlap with NftWon. results.flow_summary: Normal prize deposit that turns on the raffle. RaffleFactory.createRaffle initializes a new clone in AwaitingPrize, then calls safeTransferFrom on the ERC-721 the sponsor picked. A standards-compliant token moves ownership to the clone and calls Raffle.onERC721Received with operator=factory, from=sponsor and tokenId=prizeTokenId. All five checks pass, so the hook sets status to Active, emits PrizeDeposited and returns the magic selector. The factory then reads ownerOf and status again and emits RaffleCreated. The flow ends with a stored Active raffle that is open for USDC entry sales.
results.flow_input_to_sink: msg.sender (the token at the sponsor's params.prizeToken), operator (the factory, as the token's _msgSender()), from (the createRaffle caller/sponsor) and tokenId (params.prizeTokenId) are each checked for equality against values the factory stored from the same sponsor call. The data argument ("") is ignored. Only the pass/fail result reaches the status write. msg.sender, tokenId and from are logged in PrizeDeposited.
results.flow_terminal_action: Writes status = Status.Active to the new clone's storage (Raffle.sol:428) and emits PrizeDeposited. createRaffle then finishes and emits RaffleCreated, which opens USDC entry sales.
results.flow_security_relevance: This is the only AwaitingPrize->Active transition, so it gates every later money flow: entry sales, settlement and prize delivery. The hook never checks custody itself. It relies on the caller's identity and on arguments the token supplies, and the factory's later ownerOf check is answered by the same sponsor-chosen contract.

results.flow_summary: Re-entry window after activation. The hook sets the clone to Active while still running inside the prize contract's safeTransferFrom call, and it holds no raffle reentrancy lock. Code the token controls, or a contract it calls such as a contract sponsor, can therefore call back into the now-Active clone before the factory runs its ownerOf and status checks and emits RaffleCreated. Calls that only need Active, such as buyEntries, succeed and persist if creation completes. Calls that change the status (enableRefunds) make the factory revert, and a second hook call is rejected.

results.flow_terminal_action: State changes made by re-entry on the newly activated clone: USDC pulled into the clone, a ticket minted, and totals and unsettledPot updated. These persist if the factory's post-checks pass. A transition such as Refunding makes createRaffle revert.
results.flow_security_relevance: The activation write happens inside an untrusted external call, before the factory verifies the escrow and emits the creation event. This creates a window in which protocol state can change on a raffle that has not yet been fully verified or announced. results.flow_summary: Rejection during creation. While the clone is in AwaitingPrize inside createRaffle, the prize contract (or another contract acting for it) calls the hook with values that do not match exactly: a different caller address, tokenId, from or operator. Examples are non-standard tokens that pass from or tx.origin as operator, tokens split into a front contract and a separate core contract, and wrappers that remap token IDs. The hook reverts with UnexpectedPrize, the revert propagates up through the token transfer, and the whole createRaffle transaction is undone, including clone deployment, initialization, registry writes and raffleCount. If the token swallows the revert or never calls the hook, the factory's status check reverts instead.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The token-reported operator, from and tokenId, plus the calling address, are checked for exact equality against the stored factory, sponsor, prizeTokenId and prizeToken. The mismatching values are copied into the UnexpectedPrize revert data.
results.flow_terminal_action: The entire createRaffle transaction reverts, either with the propagated UnexpectedPrize or with PrizeEscrowVerificationFailed. No clone, registration or AwaitingPrize state remains.
results.flow_security_relevance: This keeps creation atomic: a clone that is initialized but not funded must never persist or stay registered. The strict five-way equality also decides which prize contracts can be raffled at all. When a token suppresses the hook's revert, re-reading status in the factory is the fallback safeguard.

results.flow_summary: Accepted wrapper callback, reserve met. The wrapper relays the clone's single outstanding request ID with exactly one word before drawRequestedAt + 2 days, while status == Drawing and no request is in flight. The handler sets winningEntry = randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1, records resolvedAt and, because totalEntries >= reserveEntries, writes status = NftWon. It then emits RaffleResolved and returns. The flow ends as a storage-only resolution. It opens permissionless settlement (5% treasury, 95% sponsor) and NFT redemption by the current owner of the winning ticket, and it permanently closes enableRefunds and releaseSponsorPrize.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The wrapper-relayed VRF word randomWords[0] becomes randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1, stored in the uint128 winningEntry. requestId is checked for equality with vrfRequestId and becomes a RaffleResolved topic. The fulfillment block.timestamp is compared with callbackDeadline and stored as resolvedAt. The NftWon outcome depends only on the stored totalEntries >= reserveEntries, not on the callback input.
results.flow_terminal_action: Writes winningEntry, resolvedAt and status = NftWon to storage and emits RaffleResolved(requestId, winningEntry, NftWon). The callback makes no external call and moves no assets. The NFT moves only later, through redeemWinningTicket.
results.flow_security_relevance: This is where the winner is chosen for the reserve-met branch, and the choice cannot be undone. The VRF word alone decides which entry wins, and so which ticket's current owner can later burn it for the escrowed NFT; the sponsor and treasury split follows from it. Points to review: the guard as a whole; the deadline boundary (strict < here, >= in enableRefunds); possible off-by-one or bias in the modulo mapping against the inclusive, 1-based ticket ranges; the uint128 cast; and irrevocability, since leaving Drawing makes later callbacks no-ops. Tickets stay transferable during Drawing (_update :497-502), so whoever holds the winning ticket at redemption is paid. The VRF output can be computed from the pending fulfillment transaction before it is included.

results.flow_summary: Accepted wrapper callback, reserve missed. The callback is validated and winningEntry derived exactly as in the reserve-met case, but totalEntries < reserveEntries, so status = CashWon. The flow ends as a storage-only resolution. It opens settlement that allocates 80% of the gross pot to the winning ticket, 5% to the treasury and the rest to the sponsor; cash redemption by the current owner of the winning ticket; and permissionless return of the escrowed NFT to sponsorRecipient. Refunds become permanently unavailable.
results.flow_input_to_sink: randomWords[0] is mapped modulo totalEntries into the uint128 winningEntry, which decides which ticket can claim the 80% cash allocation. requestId is checked for equality with vrfRequestId. block.timestamp is checked against the deadline and stored as resolvedAt. The CashWon branch comes from stored totalEntries < reserveEntries.
results.flow_terminal_action: Writes winningEntry, resolvedAt and status = CashWon to storage and emits RaffleResolved(requestId, winningEntry, CashWon). The callback makes no external call. Cash, sponsor and protocol transfers and the NFT's return to the sponsor all happen later, in separate transactions.
results.flow_security_relevance: This callback decides the reserve-missed money branch. It makes the escrowed NFT releasable to the sponsor and gives 80% of the gross pot to whichever ticket contains the selected entry. The branch is decided by the >= comparison at :521 (exactly meeting the reserve counts as met) and is fixed once status leaves Drawing. It also permanently closes the refund branch. Points to review: the boundary handling, and whether the later cash allocation and NFT return stay consistent with the result recorded here.

results.flow_summary: Late callback ignored. The authenticated wrapper callback arrives at or after callbackDeadline() (drawRequestedAt + 2 days) while status is still Drawing, or after someone has already called enableRefunds and moved status to Refunding. The handler emits VrfCallbackIgnored and returns without reverting or writing state, so the randomness is thrown away. The sold raffle then follows (or has already followed) the refund branch: full per-entry refunds to ticket owners and return of the prize to sponsorRecipient. requestDraw requires Active, so a raffle can never make a second request.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The fulfillment block.timestamp, which depends on when the oracle network fulfills, is compared with drawRequestedAt + 2 days. requestId is emitted as an indexed topic. randomWords is not used.
results.flow_terminal_action: Emits VrfCallbackIgnored(requestId, vrfRequestId, status) and returns normally. No state changes and the randomness is discarded. The raffle can only end in refunds and the return of the prize to the sponsor.
results.flow_security_relevance: This is the time boundary between resolving the raffle and refunding it. The callback is accepted only strictly before drawRequestedAt + 2 days, and enableRefunds from Drawing requires block.timestamp >= that same deadline, so the two paths should exclude each other at every timestamp, including inside a single block. The wrapper's one request is spent and the raffle has no way to re-request. Oracle latency (or reorg and ordering against an enableRefunds transaction) therefore decides between a winner and full refunds, which makes this boundary and the matching refund accounting key review points.

results.flow_summary: Mismatched authenticated callbacks ignored as a safeguard. Four cases are ignored with VrfCallbackIgnored and no state change: (1) a callback delivered synchronously during requestDraw's wrapper call, while _requestInFlight is true and vrfRequestId is not yet stored; (2) a repeat callback after resolution, when status is NftWon or CashWon; (3) a requestId different from the stored vrfRequestId; (4) randomWords.length != 1. The canonical wrapper should never produce these, because it fulfills each request once, in a later transaction, to the requesting contract, with the one word requested. This branch is therefore a backstop against wrapper misbehavior, not a normal production path.
results.flow_input_to_sink: requestId is compared with the stored vrfRequestId (still 0 while the request is in flight) and emitted as a topic. randomWords.length is compared with 1. _requestInFlight and status are read from storage. The contents of randomWords are discarded.
results.flow_terminal_action: Emits VrfCallbackIgnored(requestId, vrfRequestId, status) and returns normally. A resolved result stays fixed; an unresolved raffle stays in Drawing, waiting for the matching callback or for callbackDeadline and then refunds.
results.flow_security_relevance: These checks keep each raffle to one request and one resolution. They stop a re-entrant synchronous callback from resolving the raffle before vrfRequestId is stored (the external call at :257 happens after status is set to Drawing). They also stop any later wrapper call from re-rolling a resolved winner, or resolving with another request's ID or the wrong number of words. If a wrapper misbehaved, ignoring instead of reverting would leave the raffle in Drawing until callbackDeadline, after which only refunds are possible. This is a liveness consequence, not a change to the winner.

results.flow_summary: Any EOA or contract sends a plain native transfer (empty calldata, any msg.value including 0) to a published raffle clone. The ERC-1167 runtime has no CALLVALUE guard and DELEGATECALLs the fixed Raffle implementation with the empty calldata, keeping msg.sender and msg.value and running in the clone's storage. Solidity dispatch selects receive() because calldata is empty; neither Raffle nor any of its bases (ERC721, Context, ERC165, ReentrancyGuard, VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase) defines a fallback. receive() always reverts with DirectNativeTransfer(). It reads and writes no storage, emits nothing and makes no external call. The clone copies the 4-byte return data and REVERTs, so the transfer fails atomically and the ETH stays with the sender. The behavior is the same in every Status: AwaitingPrize (only briefly, inside createRaffle), Active, Drawing, NftWon, CashWon and Refunding. Gas caveat: with only a 2300-gas stipend (Solidity transfer/send) and a cold implementation address, the clone runs out of gas at DELEGATECALL (2600 gas for a cold account) before receive() runs. The value is still rejected, but the revert data is empty. If the implementation is already warm, the custom error comes back.
results.flow_input_to_sink: Attacker-chosen msg.value (any amount, including 0) with empty calldata, passed unchanged through DELEGATECALL to Raffle.receive(), which never reads it before reverting
results.flow_terminal_action: Revert with custom error DirectNativeTransfer(), passed up through the ERC-1167 clone; the native transfer is rejected and nothing in the clone changes
results.flow_security_relevance: Apart from payable requestDraw (Raffle.sol:240), this is the clone's only native-value entry point. It stops plain transfers from leaving unaccounted ETH in a clone that has no rescue or withdraw path. No in-repo production component pushes empty-calldata value to a raffle: not the factory, not USDC, and not the VRF consumer base, which sends exactly the quoted requestPrice. So the unconditional revert cannot block a legitimate path. Reviewers should note that receive() does not stop forced ETH, such as a SELFDESTRUCT beneficiary or ETH sent to the CREATE-derived clone address before it is deployed. That ETH sits in the balance unaccounted. Only getBalance() (a view) reads address(this).balance, and requestDraw spends only amounts covered by msg.value (Raffle.sol:258).

results.flow_summary: A contract calls requestDraw with msg.value above the wrapper quote. The raffle refunds the excess with a low-level call that sends empty calldata and all remaining gas. From its receive() or fallback, the contract sends a plain native transfer back to the raffle clone, which is msg.sender of its frame. This re-enters the raffle while the ReentrancyGuard is ENTERED and requestDraw's state is half-written: status=Drawing, drawRequestedAt set, vrfRequestId recorded, _requestInFlight cleared, and the wrapper already paid. receive() has no nonReentrant modifier, so it is reached, and it reverts with DirectNativeTransfer without touching that state. If the contract passes the failure up, the raffle's call returns success=false. requestDraw then reverts with NativeRefundFailed(msg.sender, excess), discarding the bounced revert data and undoing the draw request and the wrapper payment. If the contract swallows the revert, the refund completes and DrawRequested is emitted.
results.flow_input_to_sink: msg.value chosen by the attacker's contract (up to the excess it just received, or 0) with empty calldata, sent back into the raffle during the refund call at Raffle.sol:267
results.flow_terminal_action: DirectNativeTransfer revert inside the refund callback. The attacker's contract either swallows it (the draw goes ahead) or it becomes a NativeRefundFailed revert of the whole requestDraw
results.flow_security_relevance: requestDraw is the only raffle code that pushes native value to caller-controlled code, and it forwards all remaining gas. The receive() NatSpec also ties native intake to requestDraw. This flow shows that a bounced refund cannot be absorbed into the raffle balance and cannot change the half-written Drawing state. Its only effect is that the caller undoes its own draw request. requestDraw is permissionless, so anyone else can still request within the window.

results.flow_summary: A contract receives a raffle ticket through the ERC-721 receiver hook. The hook, onERC721Received, is called either by _safeMint inside buyEntries (where the buyer picks any contract as recipient) or by a ticket safeTransferFrom. From inside the hook, the contract sends a plain native transfer to the raffle clone, which is msg.sender of the hook. receive() reverts with DirectNativeTransfer. At that point buyEntries holds the reentrancy lock, the USDC has already been pulled, and totalEntries, ticketCount, the ticket range, unsettledPot and the mint have already been applied. If the hook passes the failure up, OpenZeppelin ERC721Utils re-raises the non-empty revert data unchanged (empty data becomes ERC721InvalidReceiver). buyEntries, or the ticket transfer, then reverts and all purchase effects are undone. If the hook swallows the revert and returns the selector, the purchase completes.

results.flow_security_relevance: receive() is the only raffle entry without nonReentrant that can be hit in the middle of a purchase, while the USDC pull and entry accounting are half-applied. results.flow_summary: The sponsor picks the prize ERC-721, which is untrusted. While running the raffle's prizeToken.transferFrom(address(this), ...) call, the prize contract sends a plain native transfer to its caller, the raffle clone. The call comes from redeemWinningTicket (NftWon) or releaseSponsorPrize (CashWon or Refunding). receive() reverts with DirectNativeTransfer. At that point the redemption's effects are already written: optional settlement, winnerRecipient, winnerRedeemed, the ticket burn and prizeClaimed. If the token passes the failure up, the high-level call passes it up again and the whole redemption or release reverts. If the token ignores it, execution continues to the ownerOf delivery check. results.flow_security_relevance: This flow crosses the untrusted-prize trust boundary. How the sponsor-chosen prize contract handles the rejected bounce decides whether a third party's prize delivery reverts: the winner's NFT redemption or the sponsorRecipient's prize return. receive() changes nothing itself, so this flow documents how the native-transfer rejection interacts with redemption liveness. It gives the token no capability beyond reverting directly.

output_json.stub_explanation: No supported vulnerability in this flow. The only way into Raffle.fulfillRandomWords (Raffle.sol:509) is VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.rawFulfillRandomWords. That function checks msg.sender for strict equality against the immutable i_vrfV2PlusWrapper (VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol:103-104) before anything else runs. The immutable is set once in the implementation constructor, which takes the address through _validatedVrfWrapper (Raffle.sol:157, 610-613). It is part of the implementation's runtime bytecode. The ERC-1167 clones made by Clones.clone (RaffleFactory.sol:106, standard 0x5af4 DELEGATECALL stub) run that same code and keep the original msg.sender, so a clone cannot be given a different wrapper and a caller cannot change its own msg.sender. Raffle has no fallback, delegatecall, arbitrary-call or other path to the internal handler: receive() reverts, the only low-level call is the native refund to msg.sender in requestDraw, and Solidity rejects selector collisions at compile time. Calldata that is not valid ABI reverts in the decoder. The canonical wrapper sends each callback only to the contract that made the request (callbackAddress = requester). So other users' wrapper requests never reach a raffle, and coordinator request IDs are unique per nonce. Someone who copies the oracle's public proof from the mempool and relays it can only deliver the one valid VRF output, still through the wrapper, so they cannot choose the random word. Inside the handler, the _requestInFlight, Drawing-status, requestId == vrfRequestId, single-word and deadline guards stop synchronous, duplicate, stale and late resolution. requestDraw can run only once (Active -> Drawing). totalEntries is always above zero, and the modulo and uint128 cast cannot overflow, so the authenticated callback cannot be made to revert or be blocked. The locked implementation (status Refunding) and unregistered clones that anyone could deploy themselves never make a request. The remaining concern, that RaffleFactory.sol:67 only checks the wrapper address has code, needs the deployer to supply a non-canonical wrapper. That is an unsupported misconfiguration: DESIGN.md names the Chainlink wrapper as a trusted canonical dependency of an ownerless, immutable deployment.

output_json.stub_explanation: I found no concrete vulnerability that the Chainlink VRF wrapper can trigger in the reserve-missed (CashWon) callback flow. Only the trusted wrapper can call rawFulfillRandomWords (VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol:103). Raffle.fulfillRandomWords (Raffle.sol:509-524) skips any callback that arrives while the request is in flight, outside Drawing, with a different requestId, with a word count other than 1, or at or after drawRequestedAt + 2 days. When it accepts one, it only writes storage and never reverts: totalEntries is at least 1 because requestDraw checks it at :243, so the modulo is safe, and winningEntry falls in [1, totalEntries]. The >= reserve comparison at :521 matches the spec and the IRaffle docs ('met or exceeded'). reserveEntries is at least 1 because only the factory can call initialize (:178) and the factory rejects a zero reserve (RaffleFactory.sol:178); a zero reserve would only ever produce NftWon anyway. totalEntries cannot change once Drawing starts, because buyEntries requires Active status and t < endTime. The callback deadline check (t >= deadline means ignore) and enableRefunds (t < deadline means revert) leave no overlap and no gap. Once the status is CashWon it is final: enableRefunds and refundTickets revert, and a late callback is ignored. Settlement (:533-558) allocates from unsettledPot, which equals totalEntries * 1e6, so the 80% and 5% shares are exact and the sponsor's remainder loses nothing. Only one ticket range can contain winningEntry, and ticket ranges persist after burns. output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable bug found in the late-callback flow. (1) The time boundary is exact. Raffle.sol:512 lets a callback resolve only while block.timestamp < drawRequestedAt + 2 days. enableRefunds from Drawing (:289-291) needs block.timestamp >= that same callbackDeadline(). Every transaction in a block sees the same timestamp, and timestamps never go backwards. So in any block only one of the two paths can change state, and transaction order inside a block cannot produce both a winner and refunds. Status also never moves backwards: Drawing goes only to NftWon/CashWon (callback) or Refunding (enableRefunds), requestDraw needs Active, and enableRefunds needs Active or Drawing. (2) An attacker cannot push an on-time callback into the ignore branch. rawFulfillRandomWords accepts calls only from i_vrfV2PlusWrapper. _requestInFlight is true only inside the atomic requestDraw call (:254-260). vrfRequestId is the wrapper's own return value. numWords is fixed at 1. The resolve path makes no external calls, has no loops, and cannot overflow (randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 <= uint128 max, and totalEntries > 0 is enforced at :243). It uses far less gas than the 300,000 callback limit, so it cannot revert or run out of gas. Nothing the sponsor controls (prize token, sponsorRecipient) is touched during fulfillment. (3) Ignoring a late callback is the documented design (DESIGN.md: callback accepted strictly before request timestamp + 2 days; refunds open at the deadline). A callback only arrives 2+ days late if the trusted Chainlink wrapper or oracle stalls (for example a long gas-lane or subscription outage). No ticket holder, sponsor or requester can cause that. Knowing the randomness from the mempool does not help before the deadline either, because enableRefunds reverts until then. (4) Refund accounting after the ignore path is sound. enableRefunds sets remainingRefundLiability = unsettledPot, which equals the sum of entries x ENTRY_PRICE over all minted tickets, and no ticket can be burned before Refunding. refundTickets checks ownership, burns each ticket, and reverts the whole batch on a duplicate ID. The liability subtraction is checked arithmetic. releaseSponsorPrize can run only once because of the prizeClaimed flag. Nothing is overpaid or stranded; the only loss is the VRF fee the requester paid, which is by design.

output_json.stub_explanation: No concrete vulnerability in the ignored-callback branch at packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:510-516. (1) Authentication: rawFulfillRandomWords (VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol:101-106) only accepts msg.sender == i_vrfV2PlusWrapper. That value is a nonzero immutable baked into the implementation bytecode, so every ERC-1167 clone checks the same wrapper. The canonical v2.5 wrapper sends each callback to the address that made the request (msg.sender of requestRandomWordsInNative, or the LINK transferAndCall sender). No third party can register a request that calls back this raffle. (2) Only one request per raffle: status can only move AwaitingPrize -> Active -> Drawing -> {NftWon, CashWon, Refunding}, or Active -> Refunding. requestDraw requires Active, so it can run only once and nothing returns the raffle to Active. The canonical wrapper therefore delivers exactly one callback, with the stored requestId and one word, in a later transaction. Cases 1-4 (in-flight, already resolved, wrong id, wrong length) can only happen if the trusted wrapper misbehaves, which is outside the stated trust model. Even then they change no state, and the || short-circuit means randomWords[0] is never read. (3) _requestInFlight cannot get stuck: it is set at :254 and cleared at :260 in the same transaction, and a revert rolls it back. During the native refund call at :267 an attacker cannot make the wrapper call back. That would need an oracle VRF proof, and the coordinator cannot fulfill in the same block because the blockhash is not yet available. The other nonReentrant functions are locked. (4) The late-callback check (block.timestamp >= callbackDeadline()) uses the same boundary as enableRefunds' Drawing branch (block.timestamp >= callbackDeadline()). So a callback before the deadline resolves the raffle, refunds open at the deadline, and there is no overlap or race. (5) Ignoring instead of reverting has the same effect on the wrapper, which deletes the callback and never retries. The worst case is the designed fallback to refunds, which is a liveness outcome and does not change the winner. The callback path makes no external calls and uses far less than the 300,000 gas limit.

output_json.stub_explanation:
I found no concrete vulnerability that an attacker can exploit in the prize-deposit hook at Raffle.sol:416-431.

1. The hook only accepts a call while status == AwaitingPrize. That state exists only inside RaffleFactory.createRaffle, which is nonReentrant, between initialize (Raffle.sol:205) and the prize safeTransferFrom (RaffleFactory.sol:128). The factory then requires ownerOf == raffle and status == Active. Any failure reverts the whole creation, including the clone deployment and the isRaffle registration. No code path can set AwaitingPrize again.
2. The implementation contract is locked as Refunding. A rogue, uninitialized clone has prizeToken == address(0), so its msg.sender check can never pass.
3. Four equality checks protect the hook: msg.sender must be the configured prizeToken, tokenId must be prizeTokenId, from must be the sponsor, and operator must be the immutable factory. The factory always uses msg.sender as the transfer source, so nobody can escrow an NFT they do not own. Because operator must be the factory, which is locked, nobody else can trigger a second valid hook call. This covers third parties called by transfer hooks and a sponsor calling safeTransferFrom directly. Unrelated safe transfers are rejected.
4. Reentering during the deposit window does not help an attacker:
   - createRaffle is locked against reentry.
   - initialize can only run once.
   - Before activation, buyEntries, requestDraw and enableRefunds all reject AwaitingPrize.
   - After activation, only harmless or self-reverting actions are possible: entry purchases, or a sponsor-only refund that makes the factory's status check revert.
   - isRaffle is only ever used to block destinations. It never grants privileges, so registering before escrow cannot be abused.
5. The only way to activate a raffle without real custody is for the sponsor to deploy a dishonest ERC-721 that calls the hook itself and lies in ownerOf. That gives the sponsor nothing beyond raffling a worthless NFT they deployed, which the protocol already allows by design, and the emitted prizeToken address shows buyers which contract it is. No on-chain custody check can prevent it, because the same contract answers that check. It is also outside the documented assumption that prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s (IRaffle.sol:14-15).

output_json.stub_explanation: The described sequence does work mechanically, but it gives an attacker nothing they don't already have by choosing the prize token, and no raffle-side fix could stop it. (1) Raffle.onERC721Received (Raffle.sol:416-431) only succeeds while status == AwaitingPrize. That state exists only inside RaffleFactory.createRaffle, between initialize (Raffle.sol:205) and the factory's checks after the transfer (RaffleFactory.sol:128-134). The hook also requires msg.sender == prizeToken, so only the prize contract the sponsor chose can fake it. If a third party triggered it first, the token's real hook call would hit status Active, revert, and roll back the whole creation. Direct calls from EOAs, unrelated NFTs, mints (from == 0) and calls to the implementation (status Refunding) are all rejected. (2) For an honest ERC-721, operator == factory can only come from the factory's own safeTransferFrom, and the factory's ownerOf check (RaffleFactory.sol:129) confirms real custody. So a real prize cannot be faked. (3) For a malicious token, that contract is the only record of who owns the NFT. A balance or ownerOf check inside the hook would get the same false answer, and the token could also add a backdoor to move a really deposited NFT out later. The raffle cannot tell a faked escrow from a real one, so there is no missing check to add. (4) The harm is the same as a sponsor honestly depositing a worthless, fake-metadata or backdoored NFT from a collection they deployed themselves. Buyers end up in an NftWon outcome that pays 95% to the sponsor for a worthless prize. The protocol accepts this risk explicitly: IRaffle.sol:14-15 says 'Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s', and buyers can read prizeToken() on-chain before buying. (5) The malicious token cannot reach anything beyond its own prize. It cannot touch USDC accounting (buyEntries, settlement and refunds never call it), the treasury's 5%, refunds, other clones or the factory. Every function that changes state is nonReentrant or guarded by initialized/status, and the hook rejects every call after activation.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability: unrelated callers cannot use the onERC721Received check at Raffle.sol:422 to change anything. (1) Only initialize (Raffle.sol:205) sets status to AwaitingPrize. It runs once, only when called by the factory (Raffle.sol:177-178), and only on a clone that createRaffle has just made. The same transaction reverts unless the clone is Active by the end (RaffleFactory.sol:132-133), so no registered clone stays AwaitingPrize. Nothing else sets that status: the other writes are at lines 165, 252, 299, 428 and 521. (2) The implementation's constructor sets it to Refunding with prizeToken = address(0) (Raffle.sol:164-165). (3) A third-party ERC-1167 clone starts in status 0 (AwaitingPrize), but it can never be initialized, so prizeToken stays address(0) and no real msg.sender can match it. (4) The only point when a clone is AwaitingPrize is inside createRaffle, while the sponsor's chosen prize token runs safeTransferFrom. Any other contract called during that window fails the msg.sender == prizeToken check, and the prize token itself is the sponsor's own choice. (5) A foreign NFT, a different tokenId from the prize collection, or a direct call from an EOA or contract all fail the status check or the msg.sender check. They revert with UnexpectedPrize before any storage write or event, and OZ ERC721Utils passes that revert back so the sender's transfer fails. (6) The hook makes no external calls. factory, quoteToken and i_vrfV2PlusWrapper are immutables built into the implementation's bytecode and shared by every clone. output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability found in this flow. Raffle.receive() (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:171-173) reverts with DirectNativeTransfer() on every call. It reads and writes no storage, emits nothing and makes no external call, and the ERC-1167 clone (Clones.sol:54-57) passes that revert up, so the sender keeps their ETH in every Status. The unconditional revert cannot block a legitimate path: the factory is non-payable and clones with value 0 (RaffleFactory.sol:106), USDC sends no ETH, and the VRF consumer base sends exactly the quoted requestPrice to the wrapper and gets no native refund back. Calls with 1-3 bytes of calldata or an unknown selector also revert because there is no fallback. ETH forced in (a SELFDESTRUCT beneficiary, or ETH sent to the CREATE-derived address before deployment) stays in the balance unused. The only reader of address(this).balance is the getBalance() view. requestDraw spends only what msg.value covers (Raffle.sol:250 and :258) and refunds any excess to msg.sender, so forced ETH cannot be spent or change any accounting. Pre-funding the clone address does not stop CREATE, because only an existing nonce, code or storage at the address causes a collision. The 2300-gas stipend case only changes the revert data (out of gas at the cold DELEGATECALL); the transfer is still rejected. The attacker can only lose gas or lock their own forced ETH, so there is no victim or exploitable effect.

output_json.stub_explanation: Nothing exploitable was found. The refund call at Raffle.sol:267 only sends native value to msg.sender, the address that called requestDraw and paid msg.value. If that contract sends value back, receive() at Raffle.sol:171-172 always reverts with DirectNativeTransfer and writes no state. The bounced value cannot be absorbed and cannot change the half-written Drawing state. Other ways back in are blocked: every state-changing raffle function is nonReentrant, including buyEntries, requestDraw, enableRefunds, settle, redeem, refund and the release functions. initialize reverts because the raffle is already initialized. onERC721Received needs status AwaitingPrize, but the status is Drawing at this point. rawFulfillRandomWords only accepts calls from the trusted wrapper, and the VRF coordinator cannot fulfill a request in the same transaction without the oracle's proof. The only call the contract can still make is an ERC-721 transfer or approval on its own tickets, which is harmless. If the contract passes the failure up, Raffle.sol:269 reverts the whole requestDraw: status, drawRequestedAt, vrfRequestId and the wrapper payment are all undone. The attacker only cancels its own request and pays its own gas. If it swallows the failure, the refund has already been delivered and DrawRequested is emitted correctly. The draw cannot be re-rolled. The only new data visible in the callback is the request ID, and that does not reveal the VRF result, which depends on the oracle key and a later block hash. totalEntries is frozen once endTime passes, and status=Drawing blocks a second request. The refund call copies no return data, so there is no return-data bomb. Forwarding all gas only puts the caller's own transaction at risk. requestDraw is permissionless, so anyone else can still request within the window, and enableRefunds is the fallback if no draw is requested or no callback arrives in time. The refund amount is exact: paidPrice and the quote both come from calculateRequestPriceNative in the same transaction, and any native value forced into the raffle never enters the calculation, which uses msg.value only.

output_json.stub_explanation: I found no vulnerability in this flow. receive() at Raffle.sol:171-173 is a bare `revert DirectNativeTransfer()` and touches no storage. The contract has no fallback, so a plain transfer with any msg.value, including 0, only produces a 4-byte revert. The other functions the hook can reach without the lock also cannot change the raffle's accounting: initialize is already initialized, onERC721Received requires status AwaitingPrize, rawFulfillRandomWords accepts only the VRF wrapper, and the ERC-721 approve/transfer functions act only on the caller's own tickets and are screened by _update. ETH force-sent to the clone or implementation (for example via selfdestruct) stays stuck at the sender's own cost. Nothing reads address(this).balance, and requestDraw checks paidPrice against msg.value, so stuck ETH cannot fund a draw or change any accounting. The Chainlink v2.5 native wrapper never sends ETH back to the consumer, so the always-reverting receive() blocks no legitimate path.

results.flow_summary: Ticket owner calls transferFrom to a code-less recipient: an EOA, a precompile, or an address with no code yet. Raffle._update screens `to` against the fixed protocol addresses and factory.raffleImplementation(). Because `to` has no code, the factory isRaffle registry lookup is skipped. OpenZeppelin then authorizes the owner, clears the single-token approval, moves balances and writes `_owners[tokenId] = to`. The path has no lifecycle gate (Active, Drawing, NftWon, CashWon and Refunding all allow it), so the ticket's stored entry range and its refund or prize claim go to `to`.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The owner picks any code-less `to`. It passes the destination screen without a registry lookup and is written as the owner of the caller-chosen `tokenId`. `from` is only compared with the actual previous owner.
results.flow_terminal_action: Storage write `_owners[tokenId] = to` with balance updates and a Transfer event. From then on only the new owner can use this ticket's `_ticketRanges` claim through refundTickets or redeemWinningTicket.
results.flow_security_relevance: The factory registry is consulted only for addresses that already have code (Raffle.sol:602). Clone addresses come from the factory's CREATE nonce and are predictable, so a ticket can be sent to a future raffle clone's address before that clone exists, and it is never rescreened afterwards. A registered raffle could then own another raffle's ticket, against the stated 'never move assets between raffle clones' rule and the `_update` comment that protocol sinks are rejected before they can own a claim. Every successful transfer also hands over the whole bearer claim: refund value, or the NFT or cash prize.

Only the current owner can then call redeemWinningTicket, which reads ownerOf, sets winnerRecipient, burns the ticket, and delivers the prize. In CashWon the 80% cash allocation goes through _transferQuote, which screens again.

If the transferee cannot call redeemWinningTicket, the NFT stays locked, because releaseSponsorPrize does not allow NftWon (Raffle.sol:397) and there is no rescue path. Ownership is read once before the external prize call, and the ticket is burned before that call.

results.flow_summary: The ticket owner calls safeTransferFrom(owner, to, ticketId) where `to` has no code (an EOA or an address with nothing deployed yet). The 3-arg overload passes empty data to the 4-arg overload. transferFrom rejects only to == 0. The Raffle._update override then screens `to` against protocol sinks: it compares local values and makes one STATICCALL to factory.raffleImplementation(). It skips the isRaffle registry lookup because `to` has no code. OZ _update then authorizes the owner, clears the per-token approval, adjusts balances, writes _owners[ticketId] = to and emits Transfer. The `from` check passes, and checkOnERC721Received does nothing because `to` has no code. The ticket's bearer claim (refund right or winner-redemption right) ends up with `to`, whatever the raffle's lifecycle status.
results.flow_input_to_sink: The caller picks `to` (any code-less address that is not a screened protocol sink), and it is stored as the owner of the caller-chosen tokenId. `from` must equal the prior owner, and auth = msg.sender (the owner).
results.flow_terminal_action: Writes _owners[ticketId] = to (ERC721.sol:240) and emits Transfer. A code-less `to` now holds the ticket's refund/redemption claim without any acceptance check.
results.flow_security_relevance: Raffle._update is the only Raffle-specific control on ticket transfers, and by design it has no status gating. The bearer claim can therefore move in Active, in Drawing, in NftWon/CashWon (after the winning entry is public, before or after settlement) and in Refunding. Later, redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359) authorize only by the current ownerOf. Code-less destinations skip the isRaffle registry lookup (Raffle.sol:602) and get no ERC721Receiver check. A claim can therefore be parked at an address that later gains code, for example a clone address predictable from the factory's CREATE nonce.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in this flow. ERC721.transferFrom -> Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) -> ERC721._update only lets the owner or an operator the owner approved move a ticket, through the standard _checkAuthorized check. The registry lookup is skipped only for addresses with no code (Raffle.sol:602), and that matches current state. Raffle has no selfdestruct, and clones only delegate to that implementation, so a registered clone always has code. A code-less address therefore cannot be a registered raffle when the check runs. Existing clones, the implementation, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper and the prize token are all rejected. Sending a ticket to a future clone address (or an EOA or precompile) is the same as sending it to a burn address, and only the sender loses anything. The later clone can never move another raffle's ticket. Its only outbound calls go to its fixed quote token, its prize token (the factory requires the prize token to have code and not be a registered raffle, RaffleFactory.sol:155-161), the trusted VRF wrapper, view calls on the factory, the mint-recipient check, and the native refund to msg.sender. Sponsor proceeds, protocol fees and releaseSponsorPrize (CashWon or Refunding) do not depend on the winning ticket being redeemed. Each refund only reduces the liability for the caller's own tickets. A stranded ticket only gives up its holder's own claim, and the attacker gains nothing. Allowing transfers in every lifecycle state is an explicit design choice (comment at Raffle.sol:491).

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability. The transferFrom -> Raffle._update -> _isProtocolDestination path (Raffle.sol:497-502, 593-605) works as EIP-721 specifies: transferFrom does not check the receiver, and the caller is responsible for choosing a usable recipient. Only the ticket owner or an approved operator can move a ticket, and an approved operator can already take the ticket outright, so this path gives the actor no extra power. Sending a ticket to an unusable contract, such as a raffle clone from another factory, only harms the person who sent it. No third party loses anything: (1) settlement is permissionless and never reads ownership (settleWinningTicket at Raffle.sol:304 -> _settleWinningTicket at 533-558), and releaseSponsorProceeds and releaseProtocolFees (375-392) can be called by anyone. So in NftWon the sponsor's 95% and the treasury's 5% are always claimable, even if the winning ticket is stranded. In that outcome the NFT belongs to the winning ticket, not the sponsor. (2) In CashWon and Refunding the sponsor still gets the NFT back through releaseSponsorPrize (395-407). Only the stranded ticket's own cash claim or refund is lost. (3) NftWon and CashWon are final states, and redeemWinningTicket has no deadline, so an escrow marketplace can hand the ticket back later. (4) The other recipients named in the lead can redeem: multisigs and EIP-7702-delegated EOAs (which still sign their own transactions) can call redeemWinningTicket. The prize is sent with a plain transferFrom (Raffle.sol:334), so the winner does not need an onERC721Received hook. (5) The recipient contract is never called on this path. The factory registry lookup (isRaffle at RaffleFactory.sol:54) is a STATICCALL to a trusted immutable getter that cannot revert, so there is no reentrancy or denial of service. Minting goes through _safeMint, and other-factory raffle clones reject it in onERC721Received (Raffle.sol:421-426, because from=0 != sponsor). The only way to strand a ticket is the owner's own deliberate transferFrom.
