output_json.stub_explanation: This flow is standard ERC-721 delegated transfer that the ticket owner has to switch on themselves. Nothing in it reaches an unauthorized state. (1) Authorization: Raffle does not override approve, setApprovalForAll, _approve, _setApprovalForAll, _isAuthorized or _msgSender. So the only addresses OZ ERC721._isAuthorized (ERC721.sol:164-167) accepts are the real owner, an operator that owner approved for all tokens, or an address the owner approved for that one token. An operator can only use authority the owner granted, and the docs say operator authority is intended: Raffle.sol:495 says '@param auth Caller whose owner or operator authority is checked by ERC-721', and the design calls tickets transferable bearer claims in every lifecycle state. (2) No protocol contract can get or use approvals for someone else. Raffle never calls approve or setApprovalForAll and never calls its own transferFrom; _burn is reached only after a msg.sender == ownerOf check (Raffle.sol:320-325, 359-364). The factory makes only one sponsor-controlled external call, prize.safeTransferFrom (RaffleFactory.sol:128). It cannot target a raffle, because _validateCreateParams rejects isRaffle and raffleImplementation, and a raffle recipient would also be rejected by Raffle._update. The VRF wrapper and USDC are trusted and never call ticket functions. (3) An untrusted prize token can be an operator only if a ticket owner approves it, and even then it gains nothing from a callback. In redeemWinningTicket the winning ticket is burned before prizeToken.transferFrom (Raffle.sol:325 vs 334). releaseSponsorPrize uses no ticket state. refundTickets and redeemWinningTicket are nonReentrant. (4) Recipient screening in Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-501) covers every mint and transfer path, including transfers by an operator. OZ clears the single-token approval on every transfer and burn (ERC721.sol:227). Ticket IDs only increase and are never re-minted, so no stale approval carries over. transferFrom also reverts if `from` is not the real owner. (5) The remaining cases need the victim's own consent or only hurt the owner. Examples: a stale marketplace listing the owner left open, an owner or operator sending a ticket to a dead address, or a precomputed future clone address. In front-run sale cases the buyer's transaction simply reverts. None of these lets the stated actor take more than the owner delegated.

output_json.stub_explanation: No supported vulnerability. A caller who is not the owner or approved cannot take a ticket through transferFrom or safeTransferFrom. ERC721.transferFrom (ERC721.sol:115-125) passes _msgSender() as auth. Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) only adds a check that reverts when `to` is a protocol address, then passes `auth` unchanged to super._update. ERC721._update (ERC721.sol:216-222) reads the real owner with _ownerOf(tokenId), not the caller-supplied `from`. It then runs _checkAuthorized, which reverts with ERC721InsufficientApproval unless the caller is the owner, isApprovedForAll(owner, caller) is true, or _tokenApprovals[tokenId] equals the caller. The supplied `from` is checked separately afterwards (ERC721IncorrectOwner). Raffle does not override _isAuthorized, _checkAuthorized, isApprovedForAll, _getApproved, _ownerOf, _approve or _msgSender. Context._msgSender returns msg.sender. All 31 OpenZeppelin and Chainlink files match the SHA-256 values in dependency-hashes.json, and ERC721.sol is the standard v5.6 code. ERC721._update clears the per-token approval on every transfer and burn. Ticket IDs are sequential (ticketCount + 1) and never reused, so an old approval cannot carry over to a new ticket. The only Raffle paths that change ticket ownership without auth are _safeMint, which mints only fresh IDs in buyEntries, and _burn in redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-325) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-364). Both burns first require msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId). Duplicate IDs in a refund batch revert on the second ownerOf, so a third party cannot get a refund or prize for someone else's ticket. The recipient check only makes view calls to the immutable factory (raffleImplementation and isRaffle). It changes no state and can only add reverts, so it cannot weaken authorization. If a ticket is sent to a recipient the check does not catch (e.g. a future clone address with no code yet), only the owner's own transfer choice causes it, and no third party can trigger it.

output_json.stub_explanation: This flow has no vulnerability that the stated actor can exploit. Raffle overrides only _update; transferFrom, _ownerOf, _isAuthorized, _checkAuthorized, _approve and _msgSender are the stock OpenZeppelin v5 versions, and ERC721.sol matches the hash in dependency-hashes.json. Within transferFrom (ERC721.sol:115-125), Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) first screens the recipient with _isProtocolDestination. Those checks are plain address comparisons plus two calls to the immutable, trusted factory: raffleImplementation() and isRaffle(). Both are declared view in IRaffleFactory and are called from a view helper, so they run as STATICCALLs. They cannot change state or call back into the raffle, and they run before any storage write, so they see no provisional state. ERC721._update then reads the real owner from _owners[tokenId] and checks the caller's authority against that real owner (_checkAuthorized at ERC721.sol:221), not against the caller-supplied from. Only then does it clear the approval, move balances, write the owner and emit Transfer. transferFrom then compares the returned previousOwner with from and reverts with ERC721IncorrectOwner (line 123). The EVM rolls back every write and event from that frame. No untrusted code runs between the provisional writes and that check, because safeTransferFrom's onERC721Received hook runs only after transferFrom has returned successfully. A stale or forged from therefore cannot move a ticket the caller is not authorized for, and a mismatched from leaves no partial state. Other things checked: burns skip the recipient screen as intended; transferFrom makes no untrusted external call, so no reentrancy is possible; and a failed or out-of-gas factory call simply reverts the whole transaction.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability found in this flow; it works as the design describes. ERC721.transferFrom (OZ 5.6, ERC721.sol:115) only moves a ticket when the owner or an approved operator calls it. Every mint, transfer and safeTransfer path goes through Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497), which blocks this raffle, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token, the implementation and any registered raffle. That screen only compares addresses and makes view calls to the immutable factory, so the prize token cannot influence it. Settlement (Raffle.sol:533) can only record the one ticket whose range holds winningEntry, because ranges are contiguous and never overlap, and unminted IDs return [0,0] while winningEntry is at least 1. Redemption (Raffle.sol:320-325) requires msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId). It writes all state and burns the ticket before the external prize call, under nonReentrant. During that call the untrusted prize contract can only reach transferFrom/approve on tickets, which needs authorization; onERC721Received, which reverts outside AwaitingPrize; or rawFulfillRandomWords, which only the wrapper may call. The NFT branch has no second destination screen, but that gap cannot be exploited. The winner must be the caller, and none of the screened addresses can call redeemWinningTicket: raffle clones, the factory, USDC and the wrapper have no arbitrary-call path, and the prize token can never hold a ticket. Payouts to the sponsor and treasury come from permissionless settlement and do not depend on the winner. The prize stays locked only if the owner, or an operator they approved, sends the ticket to an address that cannot redeem. That is self-inflicted and gives no attacker leverage over another party's assets. If USDC or the prize token blocks a recipient, transferability works as a recovery path. A malicious prize token refusing delivery is a sponsor-scam scenario outside this ticket-transfer entry point and outside the stated trust model.

output_json.stub_explanation:
I found no vulnerability in this flow. When a ticket moves, its refund claim moves with it. The design intends this: DESIGN.md calls the ticket a "transferable ERC721 ticket" and says "redemption requires current ticket owner". The code comment at Raffle.sol:491 says tickets "remain transferable bearer claims in every lifecycle state", and IRaffle.sol:12-13 says the same. Only the ticket owner or an operator the owner approved can move a ticket, so redirecting the claim is an action the owner authorized.

Code evidence:
(1) transferFrom calls _update(to, tokenId, msg.sender). The override at Raffle.sol:497-502 only adds a check on the recipient and passes `auth` through unchanged. OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 ERC721._update then calls _checkAuthorized, which requires the owner, an approved-for-all operator, or the per-token approved address, and clears the per-token approval on every transfer. Raffle has no ERC2771/meta-transaction context and makes no _transfer or auth=0 _update calls. The only auth=0 burns are at lines 325 and 364, and both come after an explicit ownerOf == msg.sender check.
(2) refundTickets (lines 349-372) requires Refunding status and ownerOf == msg.sender. It computes the amount from the ticket's fixed _ticketRanges entry, which the purchase set and a transfer never changes. It burns the ticket before paying. A duplicate or already-burned ID makes ownerOf revert, so each ticket pays out at most once.
(3) Accounting is complete. unsettledPot equals the sum of every ticket's entries × ENTRY_PRICE, because only buyEntries increases it and only while Active. enableRefunds moves it in full into remainingRefundLiability and is reachable only from Active or Drawing, so settlement can never overlap with refunds. Total refunds therefore cannot exceed the liability, the subtraction cannot underflow, and a transfer cannot create a second claim.
(4) A recipient can only lose funds through its own choice, such as sending a ticket to a contract it doesn't control or to a raffle clone's future address. Nobody can move another user's ticket or block their refund.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability. A nested transferFrom while a guarded raffle call is running can only move tickets the caller already owns or is approved for, and no outer function depends on ticket ownership after its external call. (1) Only a few Raffle functions lack the nonReentrant guard: the ERC-721 transfer and approval functions; initialize and onERC721Received, which revert once the raffle is initialized and Active; and rawFulfillRandomWords, which only the VRF wrapper can call. So a re-entrant caller can do nothing except move or approve tickets it controls. (2) Each guarded function finishes its checks and state writes before handing control to untrusted code. buyEntries updates totalEntries, ticketCount, _ticketRanges and unsettledPot before _safeMint, and after the onERC721Received callback it only emits TicketPurchased. requestDraw sets status, drawRequestedAt and vrfRequestId and clears _requestInFlight before the refund call, then only emits an event. redeemWinningTicket reads ownerOf (line 320), checks msg.sender, sets winnerRedeemed and burns the winning ticket (line 325) before calling the prize contract (line 334). A nested transferFrom of that ticket therefore reverts with ERC721NonexistentToken, because _checkAuthorized runs with owner = 0 and the approval was cleared by the burn. After the prize call, only prizeToken.ownerOf is read. releaseSponsorPrize never reads ticket ownership. refundTickets reads ownership, burns, and calls only the trusted USDC token, so nothing untrusted runs there. (3) Ticket entry ranges are tied to the ticket ID, and settlement and VRF fulfillment never read owners, so a mid-call transfer cannot change entry, pot or winner accounting, or the payout destination. (4) Raffle._update still blocks transfers to protocol addresses in nested calls. (5) TicketPurchased correctly names the address that received the mint, and the Transfer logs record the later move in order. DESIGN.md states that frontend discovery is advisory. (6) An approved operator could make the same transfers outside any reentrant call, so reentrancy gives it no extra power.

output_json.stub_explanation: I found no exploitable issue in the ticket transferFrom/safeTransferFrom flow. In ERC721.sol, transferFrom (line 115) first runs the Raffle._update screen (Raffle.sol:497-502), which rejects transfers to the raffle itself, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token, the implementation and registered clones. The only step after that is checkOnERC721Received (ERC721Utils.sol:33), and once that callback returns, the code only checks the returned selector. When the recipient's callback calls refundTickets or redeemWinningTicket, it does so as the real current owner. Each of those functions takes its own nonReentrant lock, re-reads ownerOf, burns the ticket and pays out in one call. No raffle accounting is tied to the transfer, and the transfer code does not reuse any stale state afterwards, so a ticket cannot be spent twice. If the callback reverts or returns the wrong selector, the whole transaction rolls back, including any redemption it made. Approvals are cleared on transfer and on burn. The raffle never transfers its own tickets; its only callback to a ticket recipient is _safeMint inside buyEntries, which runs under the lock after all state is updated. The remaining edge cases are not attacks on anyone else: sending a ticket with plain transferFrom to a contract that cannot use it, or to an address where a clone is later deployed, only strands the sender's own ticket.

The remaining gap is a ticket sent to a not-yet-deployed CREATE clone address. That is a voluntary owner/operator action that only harms the sender. output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable issue in this flow. Raffle.sol:497 `_update` only adds a destination screen and then calls the OpenZeppelin ERC721 v5.6 authorization code. All 31 dependency files match the sha256 hashes in dependency-hashes.json, so that code is unmodified. Raffle does not override `_ownerOf`, `_isAuthorized`, `_checkAuthorized`, `isApprovedForAll`, `_getApproved`, `_approve` or `_msgSender`, and it never calls `_transfer`, `_safeTransfer` or `_update` with auth=0 except for mint and burn. For burned or never-minted tickets, `_ownerOf` returns 0. `_operatorApprovals[0][*]` can never be set because `_setApprovalForAll` rejects a zero owner. `_tokenApprovals` is cleared on burn and cannot be set for a token that does not exist, because `_requireOwned` reverts. So `_checkAuthorized` always reverts with ERC721NonexistentToken. Ticket IDs are always ticketCount+1, so a burned ID can never be minted again. Unauthorized callers revert with ERC721InsufficientApproval. A wrong `from` reverts with ERC721IncorrectOwner, which undoes the write. The destination screen is skipped for burns (to==0), so it cannot block refunds or redemptions, and it only makes view (STATICCALL) calls to the trusted factory. The receiver hook runs after all state is written. safeTransferFrom writes nothing after the hook, and redeem and refund require msg.sender == ownerOf, so re-entering from the hook gains nothing. Only the owner or an operator the owner approved can do that, so the only person harmed is the one who sent the ticket. No forge or solc toolchain was available, so this conclusion comes from reading the code, not from compiling or running tests.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability: this transfer can only hurt the ticket owner who sends it. Sending a ticket to an address with no code (an EOA, a precompile, or the predictable CREATE address of a future RaffleFactory clone, RaffleFactory.sol:106) does skip the isRaffle lookup (Raffle.sol:602) and the receiver hook (ERC721Utils.sol:32). That is standard ERC-721 behaviour, and Raffle.sol:587-589 documents it on purpose. Only the current owner or an operator they approved can make the move (OZ _checkAuthorized at ERC721.sol:221). An approved operator could already take the ticket for themselves, so sending it to an unusable address gives them no extra power. It is the same as the owner sending it to 0x…dEaD. No one else loses anything. refundTickets (Raffle.sol:349-372) pays each ticket's own entries and nothing more, so a stuck ticket only leaves its own USDC in remainingRefundLiability. settleWinningTicket and _settleWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:304, 533-558) check only the ticket's stored range, not its owner or whether it still exists. So the sponsor's 95% or 15% and the treasury's 5% are always assigned and can be paid out (Raffle.sol:375-392) even if the winning ticket is stuck. releaseSponsorPrize does not depend on tickets at all. A ticket stuck in another raffle has no effect on that raffle's state either. There is no window where a deployed clone is not yet registered: the factory sets isRaffle before the untrusted prize safeTransferFrom (RaffleFactory.sol:125-128), and initialize makes only view calls to the factory. Ticket transfers change who holds a fixed entry range, not the winning-entry draw (Raffle.sol:518). State is fully updated before the receiver callback, and all Raffle functions that change state are nonReentrant. The vendored OpenZeppelin files match dependency-hashes.json.

output_json.stub_explanation:
I found no concrete vulnerability in this flow. The recipient hook does run outside the reentrancy lock, but nothing it can do there breaks Raffle state.

1. All of OpenZeppelin ERC721._update's state writes finish before ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received calls the recipient (ERC721.sol:134-135). The authorization check, approval clearing, balance updates and `_owners[tokenId] = to` all run first. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) only adds the protocol-destination screen. Raffle does not override safeTransferFrom or transferFrom, and nothing runs after the hook except the magic-value check. So there is no half-finished state to exploit and no later step that trusts stale ownership.

2. Raffle keeps no accounting tied to ownership or balances: no per-owner entry counters, snapshots or balanceOf reads. Ticket ranges (`_ticketRanges`) belong to the ticket ID, not the owner. The only functions that read ownership are redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360). Both are nonReentrant, check `msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId)` when called, and burn the ticket before paying out.

3. If the recipient re-enters during the hook, it acts as the ticket's real current owner, with the owner's normal rights. Redeeming or refunding burns the ticket once and pays once:
   - Refund liability uses checked arithmetic (`remainingRefundLiability -= amount`).
   - Duplicate ticket IDs revert because ownerOf fails on a burned ticket.
   - `winnerRedeemed`, `prizeClaimed` and `settlementComplete` stop any second claim.
   Burning or moving the ticket inside the hook leaves ERC-721 balances consistent, because the outer `_update` has already finished.

4. The recipient cannot use the ticket temporarily and hand it back for a benefit that sticks. The only actions that use ownership burn the ticket, and if the hook returns a bad selector or reverts, the whole transaction rolls back atomically.

5. The `to` screen also applies to every nested transfer made during the hook. Raffle.sol:593-605 blocks these destinations, so a ticket cannot be moved into protocol plumbing:
   - the raffle itself
   - the factory
   - USDC
   - the VRF wrapper
   - the prize token
   - the raffle implementation
   - any registered sibling raffle

6. The other permissionless functions reachable from the hook have their own status and deadline checks, and none of them depends on the transfer in progress:
   - buyEntries
   - requestDraw
   - enableRefunds
   - settleWinningTicket
   - the release functions

7. The `data` bytes are passed through to the recipient only; Raffle never reads them. The caller pays the gas sent to their own chosen recipient. A ticket owner or approved operator gains no ability beyond what plain ERC-721 ownership already gives them.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in this flow. Raffle overrides only _update (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:497). That override screens protocol sinks, which are this raffle, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token, the implementation and same-factory raffles, before OZ's auth check and ownership write. When a recipient refuses the ticket, ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received (ERC721Utils.sol:33-47) reverts: either with ERC721InvalidReceiver or by re-throwing the recipient's own revert bytes. Either way the whole safeTransferFrom reverts. Ownership, balances, the cleared approval and anything done by reentrant calls inside the hook are all rolled back, so `from` keeps the ticket and only loses the gas they chose to spend. The hook can reenter because safeTransferFrom is not nonReentrant, but this is safe. The hook only runs after super._update has finished all state writes, safeTransferFrom writes nothing afterwards, and every reentrant path rechecks state itself (redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets require msg.sender == ownerOf, settlement is ownership-agnostic, and status gates apply). The recipient, which already owns the ticket at that point, gains nothing beyond what it could do in a separate transaction. Making a redemption conditional (redeem, then revert) gives no edge either, because the outcome is fixed on-chain and public: the winning entry is already set, and the prize or cash amount is deterministic. Inside buyEntries' _safeMint, the reentrancy guard is held, so the hook cannot call guarded functions. A foreign-factory raffle clone as recipient just reverts with UnexpectedPrize, so the ticket stays with `from`. The copy of unbounded revert data is standard OZ behaviour. It only burns gas in a transaction that reverts anyway, and it adds nothing over a recipient that simply burns its 63/64 gas allowance. Any harm would fall on an external wrapper that isn't part of this codebase. Recipients choosing whether to accept is required by EIP-721, so it is not a flaw.

output_json.stub_explanation:
The described path works as written, but it is not a vulnerability. Only the winning ticket's owner, or an operator that owner approved, can start safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:115-124, _checkAuthorized). That caller already has full ERC-721 authority to send the ticket to any address. R becomes the real bearer at ERC721.sol:240, before the hook runs. Redeeming from onERC721Received therefore equals 'transfer to R, then R calls redeemWinningTicket', done atomically. Raffle.sol:23-26 and 491-492 say tickets are meant to be transferable bearer claims in every state.

Nothing is left inconsistent or open to double-claiming:
(1) ERC721.transferFrom finishes all state changes before checkOnERC721Received, and nothing runs after the hook except the selector check.
(2) redeemWinningTicket is nonReentrant. Before any external call it sets winnerRedeemed = true, burns the ticket, and sets prizeClaimed = true or zeroes winnerProceeds (Raffle.sol:323-341). Any nested redeem hits WinningTicketAlreadyRedeemed or the guard.
(3) Settlement inside the hook gives the same result no matter who calls it. unsettledPot is frozen once the status leaves Active. Ticket ranges never overlap, so only the real winning ticket passes _requireWinningTicket. Fee, cash and sponsor splits use exact 1e6 multiples and add up to grossPot.
(4) _update and _transferQuote still screen R against protocol sinks and raffle clones. NftWon and CashWon are terminal (enableRefunds only works from Active or Drawing), so releaseSponsorPrize cannot also release the NFT in NftWon.
(5) If R's hook, the prize delivery or the selector check reverts, the whole call frame reverts, including the redemption. Value cannot be kept while the transfer is undone.
(6) The untrusted prize contract cannot own tickets (rejected at Raffle.sol:498), and by the time it is called the winning ticket is already burned.

The outer safeTransferFrom finishing for a token that was burned in the same call is cosmetic. Transfer events and balances stay consistent. No unauthorized party gains the prize, and no liability is lost or double-paid.

output_json.stub_explanation: This flow is standard OpenZeppelin ERC-721 transfer behaviour. Only the ticket owner or an approved operator can move a ticket (ERC721._update -> _checkAuthorized), and the Raffle._update override only adds a deny-list of protocol sinks. Skipping the isRaffle lookup for code-less addresses (Raffle.sol:602) does let a holder park a ticket at a predictable future clone address (CREATE nonce raffleCount+2). That only strands the holder's own claim, the same as sending it to any address nobody holds a key for. A clone deployed later at that address cannot move or redeem the ticket. Raffle has no arbitrary-call path. Its only external ERC-721 calls go to its own prizeToken, and the factory refuses a registered raffle as prizeToken (RaffleFactory.sol:159). redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets require msg.sender == ownerOf and burn the ticket before paying out, so moving a ticket cannot create a double claim, move assets between clones, or change anyone else's payout or the sponsor and treasury allocations. Allowing transfers in every lifecycle state is documented design (Raffle.sol:491). An approved operator could already take the ticket outright, so parking it is no escalation. No attacker gains anything at a third party's expense.

output_json.stub_explanation:
I found no vulnerability in this flow. The delegated ticket transfer is unmodified OpenZeppelin v5 ERC-721 behaviour, and the delegate's authority always comes from an approval the owner granted. Evidence:
(1) transferFrom (ERC721.sol:121-124) runs _checkAuthorized against the real owner from _owners[tokenId]. It then reverts unless the caller-supplied `from` equals that owner. A delegate cannot name an arbitrary victim.
(2) _isAuthorized (ERC721.sol:164-168) accepts the owner, an operator stored under _operatorApprovals[currentOwner], or _tokenApprovals[tokenId]. Operator approvals are keyed by owner, so an approval left over from an earlier owner gives no authority once the ticket moves to someone else.
(3) Every transfer and burn clears the per-token approval (ERC721.sol:227/398). Ticket IDs are sequential and never re-minted, so no stale per-token approval can apply later.
(4) Raffle.sol never sets or uses approvals on its own tickets; no approve, setApprovalForAll or _approve calls exist in src/. Neither protocol contract can be used as a confused-deputy operator:
  - The factory only calls prize.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, raffle, id). Raffle tickets are barred as prizes (isRaffle and raffleImplementation checks in _validateCreateParams).
  - A raffle only calls prizeToken.transferFrom(address(this), ...).
(5) Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) screens the recipient for every caller, including delegates.
(6) An approved operator cannot redeem or refund. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360) require msg.sender == ownerOf. Payouts always go to the current owner.
(7) The onERC721Received callback runs after ownership and balances are fully committed, with no Raffle reentrancy lock held. The recipient can only do what any new owner can. If the callback reverts, the whole transfer reverts.
The design and IRaffle docs both say tickets stay transferable bearer claims in every lifecycle state. A marketplace or contract the owner explicitly approved moving tickets is the standard ERC-721 trust model, not a missing or flawed protection.

output_json.stub_explanation:
I found no vulnerability in this flow. ERC721.safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:133-136) runs transferFrom first, and Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) screens `to` and then calls super._update. Ownership, balances, the cleared approval and the Transfer event are all committed before ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received makes the external call (ERC721Utils.sol:33). After the callback, the outer frame only compares the returned selector. It holds no stale local state and has no Raffle storage writes left to make, so reentering cannot leave Raffle in an inconsistent state.

Every Raffle function that changes value is nonReentrant: buyEntries, requestDraw, enableRefunds, settleWinningTicket, redeemWinningTicket, refundTickets and the release* functions. Each one re-reads current state and enforces its own owner, status and time checks. When the recipient calls one from inside onERC721Received, the result is the same as calling it in the next transaction. The recipient is then the real ownerOf(ticketId), so redeeming, refunding or re-transferring that ticket is its legitimate right as bearer. Settlement, the release* functions, enableRefunds and requestDraw are permissionless and time/status-gated. buyEntries pulls USDC from the caller. Nothing reachable lets the recipient touch another user's tickets, funds or the prize.

Raffle never calls safeTransferFrom on its own tickets in the middle of a guarded operation. Its only ticket callback is _safeMint in buyEntries, which runs after all state writes and while the guard is ENTERED. Prize delivery uses transferFrom on a prize token, and the factory guarantees that token is not a registered raffle.

The other callables are blocked. initialize reverts on the initialized flag, onERC721Received requires msg.sender == prizeToken while AwaitingPrize, and rawFulfillRandomWords requires msg.sender == wrapper. EIP-7702 delegated EOAs just get the callback, which is correct behaviour; a clone address cannot carry a delegation.

There is one gap in the screen: a code-less address, such as a future CREATE-derived clone address, skips the isRaffle lookup. Using it would only strand the sender's own ticket, which an owner or operator could equally do by sending it to any dead address. That is not third-party harm. Gas griefing or a reverting recipient only affects the sender's own transaction.

output_json.stub_explanation: The flow works as the lead describes, but it is the intended bearer-claim behaviour, not a vulnerability. In OZ 5.6 ERC721, transferFrom finishes every state change before handing control to the recipient: Raffle._update screens `to`, ERC721._update moves the balances and sets _owners[ticketId] = to (ERC721.sol:240), and the previousOwner == from check runs (ERC721.sol:122). Only then does safeTransferFrom call checkOnERC721Received (ERC721.sol:135). After the callback returns, the outer frame only compares the returned selector. It reads and writes no raffle state, so the open reentrancy guard leaves no stale state to exploit. While onERC721Received runs, `to` is already the real owner, the same as if it redeemed in a later transaction. The design says 'redemption requires current ticket owner', and Raffle.sol:320-321 checks exactly that. redeemWinningTicket also sets winnerRedeemed (and prizeClaimed, or winnerProceeds = 0) before any external call. That rules out a double redemption, and other nonReentrant entrypoints are blocked during delivery. Settlement is permissionless and does not depend on the caller, so the sponsor and treasury allocations are the same whoever redeems. Nobody is harmed. The sender gave the ticket away on purpose, an approved operator already has full transfer authority, and the recipient only gets the prize that belongs to the winning ticket. Balances stay consistent: the recipient's balance goes +1 then -1, and the sender's goes -1. The 'successful transfer of a ticket that no longer exists' is a generic ERC-721 property, since any receiver can burn or forward a token inside its callback. It only matters for a third-party integrator that has its own flaw, which this codebase does not show.

output_json.stub_explanation: The traced re-entry is real but does no harm. In OZ 5.6.1, ERC721.transferFrom runs _update (Raffle.sol:497-501 → ERC721.sol:216-245) and its previousOwner == from check before ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received is called. By the time onERC721Received runs, the owner, balances and approval cleanup are all done, and neither Raffle nor ERC721 reads or writes ticket state after the callback returns. So when `to` calls refundTickets (Raffle.sol:349) from inside the callback, it is already the real current owner, and the result is the same as calling refundTickets in a later transaction. The design treats tickets as bearer claims, so the recipient is entitled to this refund. refundTickets protects itself without the guard: (1) it checks owner == msg.sender for every ID (:359-360), so tickets owned by others can't be refunded; (2) _burn runs before payment (:364), and a duplicate or burned ID reverts at ownerOf, so nothing is refunded twice; (3) remainingRefundLiability is set once in enableRefunds to unsettledPot, which equals totalEntries × ENTRY_PRICE, exactly the sum of all ticket ranges × ENTRY_PRICE, and nothing else reduces it, so the checked subtraction at :368 can't be used to over-draw or harm other holders; (4) if the callback reverts or returns the wrong selector, the whole transaction reverts, refund included, so the refund can't be kept while the transfer is undone. The sender gave up the ticket on purpose, and approved operators already had that authority. Other holders, the sponsor and the treasury lose nothing, and no funds move between clones. The claimed integrator/indexer risk is not a protocol bug: events come out in order (Transfer from→to, Transfer to→0, TicketsRefunded), ticketRange data stays readable, and any integrator that checks ownerOf afterward only lets the recipient block its own transaction. The callback also can't reach this path during buyEntries, because that call holds nonReentrant and requires Active status while refunds require Refunding.

output_json.stub_explanation: I found no vulnerability in this flow. The re-entry it describes is standard ERC-721 behavior and does not break any Raffle invariant. (1) OZ ERC721 5.6.1 (ERC721.sol:115-136, 216-245) commits the whole transfer before calling ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received (ERC721Utils.sol:33): the ownership check, approval clearing, balances, _owners[tokenId] = to, and the Transfer event. When onERC721Received runs, `to` is the real owner, so forwarding the ticket, approving someone, or redeeming or refunding it is the owner acting on its own ticket. Nothing is stolen and no third party is harmed. EIP-721 does not promise that `to` still holds the token after safeTransferFrom returns. (2) The protocol-sink screen holds on every hop. Each nested transfer goes through Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-501), which rejects `next` if it is a protocol sink. If that nested call reverts, the revert passes back up through checkOnERC721Received, or the recipient catches it and the forward never happens. Either way no ticket ends up owned by a sink. (3) Unscreened approvals are harmless. Approving or setting an operator does not change ownership, and none of the sink contracts ever calls transferFrom on a ticket: the raffle itself, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the implementation and other clones. The factory rejects raffle clones and the implementation as prize tokens (RaffleFactory.sol:157-162), so no clone or factory code path ever moves another raffle's tickets. (4) No code in the repo depends on who owns the ticket after a transfer. Raffle never transfers tickets itself; it only mints them (_safeMint inside nonReentrant buyEntries, followed only by an event) and burns them. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-325) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-364) read ownerOf at call time and burn right away, before any external call. The factory re-checks ownerOf after its own prize transfer. (5) The nesting depth is bounded by gas the caller pays for and has no effect on the protocol. The remaining concern, outside integrators that assume ownership after safeTransferFrom, is hypothetical: no such code exists in this snapshot, and DESIGN.md says transaction decisions must reread current chain state.

output_json.stub_explanation: The recipient veto is standard OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC-721 behaviour, and the Raffle adds no exploitable state around it. The vendored OZ files match dependency-hashes.json. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) only screens out protocol destinations and then calls super._update; nothing in safeTransferFrom runs after checkOnERC721Received. If `to` rejects the ticket, whether by wrong selector, empty revert, running out of gas, or a bubbled reason (ERC721Utils.sol:32-46), the whole transaction reverts. Ownership, balances and the cleared approval go back to their prior state, along with anything the callback did. If `to` accepts, it is the legitimate owner at callback time. Any redeem or refund it makes during the callback (both nonReentrant and owner-checked, Raffle.sol:309-372) is something it could do directly, and the state is consistent at that point. The only party that pays gas or suffers the veto is the owner or approved operator who picked `to`. The Raffle never pushes tickets to untrusted recipients on its own paths. The only one is _safeMint to the buyer's chosen recipient in buyEntries, after all state updates and under nonReentrant. Refunds and redemption burn tickets, prize delivery uses plain transferFrom, and USDC goes out through SafeERC20 (Raffle.sol:235, 334, 404, 566). So a rejecting recipient cannot block settlement, refunds, sponsor or treasury releases, or other users. Copying a large revert payload only costs the caller who chose the recipient. Rejection by contracts and 7702-delegated EOAs is a usability limit, and transferFrom remains available. No third-party loss, fund lock or bypass of protocol invariants is reachable.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability was found in this flow. The Raffle._update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) runs _isProtocolDestination before super._update. That check compares `to` with the local sinks and then makes STATICCALLs to the immutable factory. raffleImplementation() is an immutable getter and isRaffle() is a mapping getter, so neither call can revert or be manipulated. Every registered clone is a CREATE-deployed minimal proxy that always has code: Raffle has no selfdestruct or arbitrary delegatecall. createRaffle registers the clone (RaffleFactory.sol:125) before any untrusted code runs (the prize safeTransferFrom at :128). Between Clones.clone (:106) and registration, the only external call is initialize, which makes only factory view calls. So the implementation and every existing sibling clone are always rejected. Three gaps remain: counterfactual future-clone addresses (the CREATE nonce is predictable), uninitialized clones of the implementation deployed by someone else, and clones from other factory deployments. Each only lets the ticket owner, or an operator they approved, strand that owner's own ticket. That is no different from sending it to any address with no key, and it needs no protocol flaw. No third party loses anything. Settlement is permissionless and storage-only, so it does not depend on who holds the ticket. Sponsor and treasury claims are independent of the ticket holder. Refunds of other tickets are unaffected. A clone that holds a foreign ticket can never move it, because a clone only calls its own prizeToken, and the factory requires the prize token to have code and rejects isRaffle[prizeToken]. The onERC721Received callback runs only after the ownership update has fully finished, and nothing is read after it, so reentry sees consistent state. The extra gas from the two view calls is not a security issue.

output_json.stub_explanation:
No exploitable flaw in this flow. The ticket authorization boundary is the stock OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC721 `_checkAuthorized`/`_isAuthorized` (ERC721.sol:164-187), and the vendored file's SHA-256 matches dependency-hashes.json. Raffle does not override `_isAuthorized`, `_checkAuthorized`, `_approve`, `_ownerOf`, `isApprovedForAll`, `getApproved`, `transferFrom`, `safeTransferFrom` or `_msgSender`. It never uses `_transfer` or `_safeTransfer`. Its only override, `_update` (Raffle.sol:497-502), runs a recipient screen and then passes `auth` (msg.sender) unchanged to `super._update`. That screen only makes view calls (STATICCALL) to the immutable trusted factory getters `raffleImplementation` and `isRaffle`. It does not change state or give anyone authority, so running it before the authorization check is harmless.

Unminted and burned tickets cannot be moved. Their `_owners` entry is 0. `_tokenApprovals` cannot be set because `approve` calls `_requireOwned`, and `_update`/`_burn` clear any approval. `_operatorApprovals[address(0)][*]` can never be true because `_setApprovalForAll` rejects a zero owner. So `_isAuthorized` is always false and the call reverts with ERC721NonexistentToken. A burned ID cannot be revived: ticket IDs come from the monotonically increasing `ticketCount` (checked `++`), so an ID is never minted twice. Tickets are burned only in `refundTickets` and `redeemWinningTicket`, and both first check that `msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId)`.

The ranges kept after a burn in `_ticketRanges` are only read by `refundTickets` (which needs ownership first) and `_settleWinningTicket`. Settlement is only possible in NftWon or CashWon, before any burn can happen in those states, and Refunding is a terminal state, so the kept ranges grant no transfer or claim authority. The locked implementation is constructed in Refunding with `initialized = true`, so it never mints tickets. The recipient's `onERC721Received` callback runs only after ownership has fully changed, so re-entering `redeemWinningTicket` or `refundTickets` from it is the legitimate new owner acting. No third party can transfer, revive or redirect a ticket through this path.

output_json.stub_explanation: The flow is safe as traced, and there is no supported vulnerability. safeTransferFrom(from, address(0), id) calls the 4-arg overload (ERC721.sol:129), which calls transferFrom at :134. transferFrom reverts with ERC721InvalidReceiver(address(0)) at ERC721.sol:116-117, before Raffle._update runs, so nothing changes. output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable bug in this flow. The OpenZeppelin files it touches (ERC721.sol, ERC721Utils.sol, Context, draft-IERC6093) match the SHA-256 hashes in dependency-hashes.json, so this is the stock OZ v5.6 code. Raffle overrides only _update (plus pure name/symbol); it does not override transferFrom or safeTransferFrom. Path: safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:128) -> safeTransferFrom(...,"") (:133) -> transferFrom (:115). transferFrom rejects to==0, then calls the virtual _update(to, id, msgSender) (:121), which dispatches to Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497). Raffle._update only screens `to` with _isProtocolDestination. That check reads immutables and makes STATICCALLs to the trusted, immutable factory's view getters raffleImplementation() and isRaffle(), so it writes no state and runs no untrusted code. super._update (ERC721.sol:216) then reads the real owner with _ownerOf and checks authorization against that real owner in _checkAuthorized (:221). Next it clears the approval, adjusts balances, writes _owners[id]=to (:240), emits Transfer with the true prior owner, and returns that owner. transferFrom compares the result with the caller's `from` and reverts with ERC721IncorrectOwner (:122-123). Between that state write and the revert there is no external call and no hook. checkOnERC721Received (:135) is never reached, so the untrusted recipient cannot run code while ownership is tentatively changed. The REVERT undoes every write in the Raffle call frame: approval clear, balances, owner and the log. That holds even if an outer contract wraps the call in try/catch. A wrong `from` also gives an approved operator no extra power: authorization is always checked against the real owner, and the Transfer event and receiver callback can only carry the true prior owner. Other ownership paths (_mint via _safeMint, _burn in redeem/refund) have their own return-value checks and are outside this revert path. With no unsafe state persistence, no reentrancy window and no authorization bypass, there is nothing concrete to report.

output_json.stub_explanation: The lead does not show a real vulnerability. A ticket owner can move a ticket from inside the external call of a guarded operation, but no guarded function relies on ticket ownership after that call. (1) buyEntries (Raffle.sol:209-237) writes totalEntries, ticketCount, _ticketRanges and unsettledPot, and pulls in the USDC, before calling _safeMint at :235. After the recipient callback it only emits an event. (2) In requestDraw (:240-273), the excess-fee refund at :267 happens after status, drawRequestedAt and vrfRequestId are set. Nothing after it reads ticket ownership. (3) Only two guarded functions read ticket ownership: redeemWinningTicket (:320) and refundTickets (:359). Both check the caller and burn the ticket before any external call (the prize transferFrom or the USDC transfer), so a nested transfer cannot cause a double claim, a redirected payout or a broken balance. (4) The unguarded transfer path only changes ERC-721 owner, balance and approval records. It still enforces owner/operator authorization and the protocol-sink check in Raffle._update (:497-502). Calls to guarded functions during the nested callback revert, which is the intended protection, and only the actor who chose to nest the transfer is affected. (5) IRaffle documents TicketPurchased.recipient as the address that received the newly minted ticket, which stays true. Transfer events, emitted in the correct order, are the ownership record. Tickets are bearer claims that can be transferred at any time by design, and nothing in the repo derives ownership from TicketPurchased. No on-chain asset, accounting or authorization impact is reachable.

results.flow_summary: The current ticket owner calls the inherited ERC721.approve(to, tokenId) on a Raffle clone. OpenZeppelin _approve confirms the ticket exists and that msg.sender owns it, emits Approval, and overwrites the ticket's single approval slot with `to`. Any address is accepted, and address(0) revokes. The flow ends in that storage write. Raffle adds no lifecycle gate, reentrancy guard, or destination screen to this path.
results.flow_input_to_sink: `to` is stored verbatim as the ticket's only approved spender (address(0) revokes). `tokenId` picks the slot once it passes the existence check. msg.sender must equal ownerOf(tokenId).
results.flow_terminal_action: SSTORE _tokenApprovals[tokenId] = to in the clone's ERC721 storage plus an Approval(owner, to, tokenId) event
results.flow_security_relevance: A ticket is a bearer claim on the escrowed prize NFT, the cash proceeds, or a full refund. This write gives an arbitrary address the power to move that claim, in every lifecycle state: Active, Drawing, NftWon/CashWon before or after settlement, and Refunding. Raffle screens new owners against protocol sinks but does not screen approved spenders. So an untrusted contract, such as the sponsor-chosen prize token, can be given transfer authority.

OpenZeppelin takes the owner from msg.sender, checks only that operator is non-zero, writes _operatorApprovals[msg.sender][operator] = true and emits ApprovalForAll. The flow ends at the storage write and event.

output_json.stub_explanation: ERC721.approve on Raffle clones is the unmodified OpenZeppelin 5.6 code. Raffle only overrides _update, name and symbol, and has no ERC2771 or _msgSender override. _approve (ERC721.sol:386-389) requires msg.sender to be the live owner, read from _owners, or that owner's operator. Burned tickets revert in _requireOwned, and ticket IDs are sequential and never reminted. Every transfer or burn clears the stored approval (ERC721.sol:227), so it cannot carry over to a new owner. No value-bearing path reads _tokenApprovals, getApproved or isApprovedForAll. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360) both require msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId), and settleWinningTicket only moves funds between internal ledgers. No protocol contract can act as an approved spender. Raffle never owns tickets because _update rejects address(this). Raffle never calls approve or transferFrom on its own tickets. The only external transferFrom it makes is on prizeToken, and the factory rejects any prize token that is a raffle or the raffle implementation (RaffleFactory.sol:157-161). An approved spender can only move a ticket through _update, which still screens the new owner against protocol sinks (Raffle.sol:498). It cannot redeem or refund without first becoming the owner. Approving an untrusted address, such as the sponsor's prize token, is a voluntary grant by the ticket owner and only affects that owner's ticket. If the prize token re-enters during redeemWinningTicket or releaseSponsorPrize, the burn and claim flags are already written, and nonReentrant blocks re-entry into the redeem, refund and release functions. So the actor cannot harm other ticket holders, the sponsor, the treasury or the raffle's accounting through this path.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability: the approval gate is unmodified OpenZeppelin 5.6.x code and works as intended. The ERC721.sol file matches its pinned SHA-256 in dependency-hashes.json, and the approve and _approve code is the standard OZ v5 version. In approve(to, tokenId), auth is _msgSender(). Its only ERC721 override is _update, which adds a check on the destination address and passes auth unchanged to super._update. Neither Raffle nor RaffleFactory ever calls approve or setApprovalForAll. They have no generic call or multicall path that could make the clone act on someone's behalf, and Raffle can never own a ticket because _update rejects address(this). Only these paths write the three relevant mappings. (1) _tokenApprovals is written by approve, which is gated by line 389, and by _update, which only clears it on transfer or burn. output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable bug in this flow. It also requires the caller to be the owner or an operator approved for all tickets before it writes _tokenApprovals. The only write that skips this check is the internal clear inside ERC721._update, which always writes address(0). Raffle does not override approve, _approve, _ownerOf, getApproved or transferFrom. Its _update override (Raffle.sol:497) only adds a destination check for non-burn transfers before calling super._update. super._update clears the per-ticket approval whenever the ticket had an owner, so every transfer and every burn clears it (refundTickets at Raffle.sol:364, redeemWinningTicket at Raffle.sol:325). The only mint is buyEntries (Raffle.sol:228-235), using ticketCount + 1 with a checked uint128 increment, so IDs are strictly sequential and burned IDs are never minted again. Because no approval can exist on a nonexistent ID, transferFrom from address(0) cannot pass _checkAuthorized, and isApprovedForAll(address(0), x) can never be true. A stale or pre-planted spender therefore can never mint or take over a new or burned claim. Approvals pointed at protocol addresses are harmless: the factory only calls safeTransferFrom with msg.sender as the sender and rejects registered raffles as prize tokens, and raffle clones only transfer prize tokens they own themselves. output_json.stub_explanation: No concrete vulnerability. ERC721.approve (ERC721.sol:93 -> _approve:383-398) only lets the current owner or an all-tickets operator set _tokenApprovals[tokenId]. A ticket owner can do this at any time anyway, so doing it inside a guarded callback adds no power. Raffle never uses approvals for its own logic: redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360) require msg.sender == ownerOf. Approvals only authorize standard transfers, and every transfer target is screened by the _update override (Raffle.sol:497-502). No guarded function reads ticket ownership or approval after an untrusted call. (1) buyEntries commits all accounting before _safeMint (Raffle.sol:230-233); after the onERC721Received callback it only emits TicketPurchased (Raffle.sol:236). That event's fields (buyer, original recipient, ticketId, range, amount) stay accurate. The Transfer and Approval events from the callback are logged in the correct order. (2) requestDraw's native refund call (Raffle.sol:262-270) runs after all state writes, then only emits. (3) redeemWinningTicket reads ownerOf and burns the ticket (Raffle.sol:320-325) before prizeToken.transferFrom. Burning clears the approval, and later tickets have no value in NftWon. (4) The prize token can never own a ticket, because _isProtocolDestination rejects prizeToken_. So during releaseSponsorPrize it can only move tickets a user explicitly approved it for, which it could do outside any callback too. Re-entering any accounting function is blocked because the guard is ENTERED. The event-ordering concern would only affect an off-chain indexer that ignores Transfer events. No such indexer exists in this repo, and DESIGN.md says frontend discovery is advisory and transaction decisions must reread chain state, so there is no on-chain impact.

output_json.stub_explanation: No vulnerability found in the approve -> transferFrom continuation. The authorization logic is unmodified OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC721, and the file hashes match dependency-hashes.json. approve/_approve (ERC721.sol:383-398) require the caller to be the owner or an operator, and _requireOwned stops anyone pre-approving an unminted or burned ticket. Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-502) passes `auth` through unchanged and only adds a destination screen that blocks the raffle, the factory, USDC, the VRF wrapper, the prize token, the implementation, and registered clones. Its outbound calls (USDC, the prize token, the VRF wrapper, factory views, and an empty-calldata native refund) cannot be steered into moving tickets. redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets require msg.sender == ownerOf, so an approval alone cannot redeem or refund a ticket. output_json.stub_explanation: I found no vulnerability in this flow that can be exploited or that causes concrete harm. When an approved spender calls safeTransferFrom (ERC721.sol:133-135), transferFrom and Raffle._update finish every state change first: the destination screen (Raffle.sol:498), the approval check (ERC721.sol:167), clearing the approval (ERC721.sol:227) and the new owner (ERC721.sol:240). Only then does ERC721Utils.sol:33 call the recipient's hook, and nothing after the hook relies on earlier state. The hook only checks the returned selector, and any revert rolls the whole transfer back. Because no partial state is visible, a recipient that re-enters is just the legitimate owner. It can call redeemWinningTicket or refundTickets (Raffle.sol:321, 360), which require msg.sender == ownerOf and burn the ticket atomically, or it can transfer the ticket again through the same screen. Nobody can claim twice. The only nonReentrant function that triggers a receiver hook is buyEntries' _safeMint, and it still holds the lock at that point. Raffle's own onERC721Received (Raffle.sol:416) ignores `data`. Approvals give a spender no power beyond what the owner granted. Factory consumers always use from = msg.sender (RaffleFactory.sol:128), so a third party who calls createRaffle on a factory the owner approved hits ERC721IncorrectOwner. The approval is cleared on every transfer and burn. A separately deployed factory can escrow a ticket as another raffle's prize only if the ticket owner deliberately calls it. The receiving clone runs the same code: it only releases the ticket through prizeToken.transferFrom to its winner or sponsorRecipient (Raffle.sol:334, 404), screened against this raffle's factory, and never approves, burns or redeems it. The ticket's claim has no deadline (redemption and refunds never expire), and the sponsor and treasury can still settle and withdraw without the ticket. So no value is lost, no other participant is affected and no attacker gains anything. The _isProtocolDestination screen is documented as covering only "same-factory protocol plumbing" (Raffle.sol:587), and same-factory raffle tickets are already blocked as prizes (RaffleFactory.sol:159) and as transfer destinations (Raffle.sol:603).

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability. setApprovalForAll(operator, false) behaves as ERC-721 (EIP-721) and the OpenZeppelin ERC721 v5 implementation specify: it clears _operatorApprovals[msg.sender][operator] and emits ApprovalForAll. Its only override, _update (Raffle.sol:497), just blocks transfers to protocol addresses before calling super._update. A leftover per-token approval needs an operator that the owner gave blanket authority. That operator had to call approve() while still authorized (ERC721.sol:389), and at that moment it could already have transferred the ticket outright. An attacker could only exploit this after the victim had already given it full control of the tickets, which is not a vulnerability in this flow.

output_json.stub_explanation:
No vulnerability found. This flow is ordinary ERC-721 operator delegation, and the account that grants the approval is the only one who can grant it.

1. **Only the caller can grant approval.** setApprovalForAll (OZ ERC721.sol:105, called at :416) writes only _operatorApprovals[msg.sender][operator]. _msgSender() is plain msg.sender: Raffle has no ERC-2771 forwarder and does not override approvals. Each clone keeps its own approval storage. So any account can only hand an operator control over its own tickets in that one raffle.

2. **Transfers still check authorization.** transferFrom -> Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497) checks that `to` is not a protocol address (via the trusted factory's view functions). It then calls OZ _update, which still enforces owner, operator or token-approval authorization (_checkAuthorized at ERC721.sol:221, :167). Burned tickets cannot be moved again: the owner is zero, approvals are cleared, and an approval with a zero owner can never be set.

3. **Paying the current holder is the specified behavior.** Raffle.sol:491-492, IRaffle.sol:12-13 and DESIGN.md all describe tickets as transferable bearer claims in every lifecycle state. They state that redemption and refund go to the current ticket owner. So an operator moving a ticket and the new holder refunding it is exactly what the owner authorized. The original owner can revoke the approval at any time.

4. **Refund accounting cannot be overdrawn.** Ticket ranges together cover exactly totalEntries, and remainingRefundLiability equals totalEntries x ENTRY_PRICE. Each ticket is burned before payment, duplicates in a batch revert, no tickets can be minted after Refunding, and the subtraction is checked. So a transfer gives the new holder only that ticket's own value, never more.

5. **Lost tickets only hurt the sender.** Moving a ticket with plain transferFrom to a contract that cannot call refund or redeem only harms the owner, or the operator the owner chose. No other user, sponsor or treasury funds are affected.

No third party can gain rights over someone else's tickets, take more than a ticket's own refund, or block other holders' refunds through this path.

step_metadata.stub_explanation: No supported vulnerability. Raffle (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:28) uses OpenZeppelin 5.6 ERC721's approval logic as shipped. Four facts rule the lead out. (1) setApprovalForAll always uses msg.sender as the owner (ERC721.sol:105-106, 409-417), so an account can only grant operators over its own tickets. (2) _approve lets the owner or an approved-for-all operator set a single-ticket approval (ERC721.sol:389). EIP-721 requires exactly this: approve "Throws unless msg.sender is the current NFT owner, or an authorized operator of the current owner". The per-ticket approval is cleared by _update on any transfer or burn (ERC721.sol:225-227), it cannot be set on unminted or burned tickets (_requireOwned, ERC721.sol:386), and the owner can clear it at any time with approve(address(0), id). (3) Keeping that approval after the operator is revoked gives no extra power. While approved, the operator could already transfer the ticket outright, so naming a spender is never more than the owner delegated. (4) Raffle-specific checks still apply to spenders. Raffle._update (Raffle.sol:497-501) checks the destination of every spender transfer. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) and refundTickets (Raffle.sol:359-360) require msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId), so an approved address cannot claim a refund or prize without first holding the ticket. Raffle never calls transferFrom, approve or setApprovalForAll on its own tickets, and makes no arbitrary external calls. Approving it or another protocol address as a spender therefore gives an attacker nothing. Approval storage is separate for each ERC-1167 clone. In short, the flow is standard EIP-721 behavior that the owner opts into, and there is no path for an attacker to take someone else's tickets.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable flaw in the setApprovalForAll / operator-transfer path. Raffle does not override setApprovalForAll, _setApprovalForAll, isApprovedForAll, _isAuthorized, _checkAuthorized or _approve. Its only ERC-721 override is _update (Raffle.sol:497-502), which screens the `to` address against protocol addresses and then calls super._update(to, ticketId, auth) with auth unchanged. So the OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 authorization logic is intact; the vendored files match dependency-hashes.json. Each transferFrom/safeTransferFrom re-reads _owners[ticketId] and checks _operatorApprovals[currentOwner][msg.sender] at call time (ERC721.sol:217-221, 164-187). Revoking takes effect immediately, an ownership change removes the old approver's operators, and per-token approvals are cleared on every transfer and burn (ERC721.sol:227). A burned or never-minted ticket can't be revived through the from==0 branch: _isAuthorized(address(0), ...) can never be true. Owner 0 is rejected at ERC721.sol:410, msg.sender is never zero, and _tokenApprovals can only be written for owned tokens and is zeroed on burn. Ticket IDs are sequential and never re-minted, so refunded or redeemed tickets can't be reused even though their ranges stay stored. A stale `from` reverts with ERC721IncorrectOwner after _update, which undoes the whole call. refundTickets and redeemWinningTicket require msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId) (Raffle.sol:320-321, 359-360), so an operator only gets the transfer authority the owner granted. Approvals live in each clone's own storage, so nothing carries over between raffles. Operators regaining control of tickets that come back to or are minted to the approver is standard ERC-721 'all assets' behavior; a third party minting to the approver pays for that ticket. An operator-set per-token approval surviving revocation is also standard EIP-721/OZ behavior, needs an operator the victim already trusted, and is not specific to this project.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable issue in this flow. setApprovalForAll is the unmodified OpenZeppelin 5.6 function (ERC721.sol:105 -> _setApprovalForAll at :409-417). It only writes _operatorApprovals[msg.sender][operator], so an account can only grant rights over its own tickets, and the operator cannot be address(0). Raffle never reads isApprovedForAll, getApproved, _isAuthorized or _checkAuthorized; grep finds no use in src/. The approval is only consumed by the inherited transferFrom, safeTransferFrom and approve. That is standard ERC-721 transfer power the owner chose to grant, and Raffle's _update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) still screens the destination of operator-initiated transfers. Every burn or payout path rechecks ownership against msg.sender. refundTickets (Raffle.sol:358-360) requires msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId) for each id before _burn, and pays msg.sender. A duplicated id reverts on its second ownerOf, so there is no double count, and remainingRefundLiability is decremented with checked arithmetic. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) requires msg.sender == ownerOf before the burn and before delivering the NFT or cash, and it pays winner == msg.sender. Any settlement done inside it at :315 is rolled back by the NotTicketOwner revert, including when an operator wraps the call in try/catch. _burn passes auth = 0 (ERC721.sol:304), but it is reachable only after these owner checks. No other path burns tickets or pays on someone else's behalf. releaseSponsorProceeds, releaseProtocolFees and releaseSponsorPrize pay fixed recipients (sponsorRecipient or protocolTreasury). settleWinningTicket only writes storage and can select only the single ticket whose stored range contains winningEntry; ids that were never minted have range (0,0) and revert. Raffle never calls its own ticket-transfer functions, so approving the raffle, factory or prize token as an operator gives them nothing. The one leftover concern: a seller with a stale marketplace listing could have a winning ticket bought cheaply after resolution. That depends on how sellers manage off-chain orders, and the design explicitly keeps tickets transferable in every state, so it is not a contract defect.

output_json.stub_explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in this flow. The reentry is real, but it gives the hook contract no power beyond what it already has. (1) Raffle.sol:235 _safeMint reaches the recipient's onERC721Received through ERC721.sol:289 and ERC721Utils.sol:33. From there the only state-changing functions that are not guarded are the inherited ERC721 approve, setApprovalForAll, transferFrom and safeTransferFrom. These check normal owner/operator authority (_setApprovalForAll(_msgSender()), _checkAuthorized), so the hook can only approve or move tickets it already owns or is approved for. Every Raffle function that changes state is nonReentrant. initialize is blocked by the initialized flag. Raffle.onERC721Received requires AwaitingPrize, the prize token as caller and the factory as operator. rawFulfillRandomWords only accepts the VRF wrapper. (2) When the hook runs, buyEntries has already finished its accounting (totalEntries, ticketCount, _ticketRanges, unsettledPot, owner) and the values are consistent. Afterwards it only emits TicketPurchased from local variables. Nothing on-chain reads ticket ownership or approvals later in the transaction. _settleWinningTicket uses only the stored ranges. redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets check ownerOf again when they are called. A transfer made inside the hook still passes the Raffle.sol:497 _update check that blocks protocol addresses. (3) Moving a ticket inside the hook has the same effect as moving it right after buyEntries returns. Tickets are designed as transferable bearer claims, and the only tickets affected belong to the hook contract, so nobody else loses anything. TicketPurchased.recipient still correctly names the address that received the mint, because Transfer(0 -> recipient) is logged first. The workspace contains no indexer, subgraph or SDK code that treats TicketPurchased as current ownership, and DESIGN.md says frontend discovery is advisory and transactions must reread chain state. (4) The native refund call in requestDraw (Raffle.sol:267) runs after status, vrfRequestId and _requestInFlight are already set. The caller can only change its own tickets or make its own transaction revert.

output_json.stub_explanation:
The flow works as the lead describes, but it does not show a vulnerability.

1. Only the owner can use the approval. A ticket owner can approve a second RaffleFactory deployment and escrow their own ticket of raffle T as the prize of that factory's clone C2. T._update only checks T's own factory, and that scope is documented ("same-factory protocol plumbing", Raffle.sol:587-605). The approval cannot be used against the owner by anyone else. RaffleFactory.createRaffle always uses msg.sender both as the transfer `from` (RaffleFactory.sol:128) and as the clone's sponsor (line 112). ERC721.transferFrom reverts unless the previous owner equals `from` (ERC721.sol:121-124), and C2.onERC721Received requires from == sponsor (Raffle.sol:423). If a third party called F2.createRaffle with the victim's ticket, it would revert with ERC721IncorrectOwner.

2. The ticket is never stranded. It becomes C2's configured prize, and C2 always reaches a state where it can release it:
   - In NftWon, the C2 winner calls redeemWinningTicket, which runs prizeToken.transferFrom(C2, winner, id) (Raffle.sol:334).
   - In CashWon or Refunding, anyone can call releaseSponsorPrize (Raffle.sol:404).
   - Permissionless enableRefunds deadlines guarantee C2 reaches one of these states (Raffle.sol:276-301).

3. T loses nothing. T's own claim paths have no expiry: refundTickets, redeemWinningTicket, and the permissionless, ownership-independent settleWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:304-372). So T's sponsor, its treasury and its other ticket holders keep full access to their proceeds, fees, refunds and prize return while the ticket is escrowed. The only effect is that the actor's own claim is delayed or exposed to C2's outcome. The actor chose this, much like listing an NFT in any escrow contract.

4. The remaining lock-up cases all need the actor's own choices, such as setting C2's sponsorRecipient to an address T rejects. They only affect the actor's own claim.

No third party loses funds, no accounting breaks, and no unauthorized transfer is possible.

json_answer.entrypoint_actor: Any EOA or contract acting as sponsor. There is no owner, allowlist or fee. The prize ERC-721 contract that the sponsor picks is an untrusted external contract, and it runs code during supportsInterface, safeTransferFrom and ownerOf.
json_answer.entrypoint_input: CreateRaffleParams calldata: sponsorRecipient (address), prizeToken (any contract address), prizeTokenId (uint256), reserveEntries (uint128), endTime (uint64). msg.sender is recorded as sponsor. The prize contract also controls its own return values and any reentrant calls it makes.
json_answer.entrypoint_label: RaffleFactory.createRaffle - permissionless raffle creation with atomic prize escrow
json_answer.entrypoint_handler: RaffleFactory.createRaffle(CreateRaffleParams) -> _validateCreateParams (RaffleFactory.sol:154, calls untrusted prizeToken.supportsInterface) -> Clones.clone(raffleImplementation) (L106) -> IRaffle(raffle).initialize (L109) -> IERC721(prizeToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, raffle, prizeTokenId) (L128) -> prize.ownerOf and raffle.status checks (L129-134)
json_answer.entrypoint_reachability: RaffleFactory has no owner and cannot be changed. It is meant for public Ethereum networks (hardhat.config.ts sepolia and mainnet; package.json deploy:sepolia). createRaffle is external and is protected only by nonReentrant and parameter validation, so any account can call it with a signed transaction to the factory address.

json_answer.flow_summary: Production success path. A sponsor calls the permissionless RaffleFactory.createRaffle, which validates the sponsor's params, deploys a fresh ERC-1167 clone and calls Raffle.initialize with msg.sender == factory. Both guards pass on the fresh storage, the one-shot flag is committed, and the zero-address checks pass (their revert can never be reached in production). The three _isProtocolDestination screens make STATICCALLs back into the factory: raffleImplementation every time, and isRaffle for destinations that have code. The clone then stores the sponsor-derived configuration and ends in Status.AwaitingPrize, and control returns to the factory for registration and prize escrow.
json_answer.flow_input_to_sink: RaffleInitParams built at RaffleFactory.sol:111-120: sponsor = createRaffle msg.sender; sponsorRecipient, prizeToken, prizeTokenId, reserveEntries and endTime copied verbatim from the sponsor's CreateRaffleParams; protocolTreasury = factory immutable; raffleId = ++raffleCount. All are written unchanged to clone storage at Raffle.sol:197-204.
json_answer.flow_terminal_action: Stores the clone's one-time configuration (Raffle.sol:197-204) and leaves it in Status.AwaitingPrize (L205). The createRaffle transaction then moves on to registration and prize escrow.
json_answer.flow_security_relevance: This is the only place where a raffle's payout sinks (sponsorRecipient, protocolTreasury), prize identity (prizeToken, prizeTokenId), escrow and cancel authority (sponsor) and lifecycle parameters are written. They can never be changed afterwards because there is no admin or setter. Authorization rests only on msg.sender == factory plus the one-shot flag. initialize adds three protocol-destination screens but no range checks, so correctness depends on the factory's pre-validation and these screens together covering every protocol plumbing address.

json_answer.flow_summary:
Re-entrant purchases during creation. The window opens after the prize contract (malicious or with transfer hooks) has activated the clone through onERC721Received and before safeTransferFrom returns to the factory. In that window the prize contract, or any contract it calls, can call the clone's buyEntries. It succeeds because:
- a fresh clone's own reentrancy guard slot is unset
- status is Active
- block.timestamp < endTime
USDC is pulled, tickets are minted (triggering the recipients' onERC721Received callbacks) and unsettledPot grows, all before the factory's post-checks. Those checks only test ownerOf and status == Active, so creation completes with entries already sold, and the TicketPurchased logs come before RaffleCreated.
json_answer.flow_input_to_sink: The re-entering contract chooses the recipient and entryCount, and pays as msg.sender. The sponsor-chosen endTime keeps the sale open.
json_answer.flow_terminal_action: Entry tickets are minted and USDC is escrowed in the clone inside the creation transaction, before RaffleCreated is emitted.
json_answer.flow_security_relevance: The factory's nonReentrant only protects the factory. Once status flips to Active, the clone's state machine is reachable mid-creation: buyEntries and the unguarded ERC-721 ticket functions. The post-conditions do not require an untouched raffle, so 'atomic creation' does not mean the raffle is empty when RaffleCreated is emitted.

In a later block, the Chainlink coordinator verifies the oracle proof and the wrapper calls rawFulfillRandomWords on the clone with the 300000 callback gas limit. The consumer base checks msg.sender == the immutable wrapper and hands off to fulfillRandomWords. The callback is accepted when the request is not in flight, status == Drawing, requestId == vrfRequestId, exactly one word is supplied and block.timestamp < drawRequestedAt + 2 days. It then stores winningEntry = randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 and resolvedAt, and sets status to NftWon (totalEntries >= reserveEntries) or CashWon, emitting RaffleResolved. No token transfer or user call happens here; settlement and redemption become available.

json_answer.flow_summary: Production success path. A sponsor calls the permissionless RaffleFactory.createRaffle, which validates the sponsor's params, deploys a fresh ERC-1167 clone and calls Raffle.initialize with msg.sender == factory. Both guards pass on the fresh storage, the one-shot flag is committed, and the zero-address checks pass (their revert can never be reached in production). The three _isProtocolDestination screens make STATICCALLs back into the factory: raffleImplementation every time, and isRaffle for destinations that have code. The clone then stores the sponsor-derived configuration and ends in Status.AwaitingPrize, and control returns to the factory for registration and prize escrow.
json_answer.flow_input_to_sink: RaffleInitParams built at RaffleFactory.sol:111-120: sponsor = createRaffle msg.sender; sponsorRecipient, prizeToken, prizeTokenId, reserveEntries and endTime copied verbatim from the sponsor's CreateRaffleParams; protocolTreasury = factory immutable; raffleId = ++raffleCount. All are written unchanged to clone storage at Raffle.sol:197-204.
json_answer.flow_terminal_action: Stores the clone's one-time configuration (Raffle.sol:197-204) and leaves it in Status.AwaitingPrize (L205). The createRaffle transaction then moves on to registration and prize escrow.
json_answer.flow_security_relevance: This is the only place where a raffle's payout sinks (sponsorRecipient, protocolTreasury), prize identity (prizeToken, prizeTokenId), escrow and cancel authority (sponsor) and lifecycle parameters are written. They can never be changed afterwards because there is no admin or setter. Authorization rests only on msg.sender == factory plus the one-shot flag. initialize adds three protocol-destination screens but no range checks, so correctness depends on the factory's pre-validation and these screens together covering every protocol plumbing address.

Re-entrant purchases during creation. The window opens after the prize contract (malicious or with transfer hooks) has activated the clone through onERC721Received and before safeTransferFrom returns to the factory. In that window the prize contract, or any contract it calls, can call the clone's buyEntries. It succeeds because:

- status is Active
- block.timestamp < endTime

json_answer.flow_security_relevance: The factory's nonReentrant only protects the factory. Once status flips to Active, the clone's state machine is reachable mid-creation: buyEntries and the unguarded ERC-721 ticket functions. json_answer.flow_summary: Asynchronous continuation: an ignored or missing callback leads to refunds. A wrapper callback is ignored when it arrives while _requestInFlight is true (a synchronous callback during L257), after status has left Drawing (a duplicate, or after refunds), with a requestId other than vrfRequestId, with randomWords.length != 1, or at or after drawRequestedAt + 2 days. If the callback is ignored, fails, or never arrives, the clone stays in Drawing until callbackDeadline. After that, anyone can call enableRefunds, which moves unsettledPot into remainingRefundLiability and sets Refunding, enabling ticket refunds and the return of the sponsor's prize. json_answer.flow_security_relevance: The accept window (strictly before drawRequestedAt + 2 days) and the refund window (at or after it) must not overlap or leave a gap. json_answer.flow_summary: A contract calls requestDraw with msg.value above the wrapper quote. The raffle refunds the excess with a low-level call that sends empty calldata and all remaining gas. From its receive() or fallback, the contract sends a plain native transfer back to the raffle clone, which is msg.sender of its frame. This re-enters the raffle while the ReentrancyGuard is ENTERED and requestDraw's state is half-written: status=Drawing, drawRequestedAt set, vrfRequestId recorded, _requestInFlight cleared, and the wrapper already paid. receive() has no nonReentrant modifier, so it is reached, and it reverts with DirectNativeTransfer without touching that state. If the contract passes the failure up, the raffle's call returns success=false. requestDraw then reverts with NativeRefundFailed(msg.sender, excess), discarding the bounced revert data and undoing the draw request and the wrapper payment. If the contract swallows the revert, the refund completes and DrawRequested is emitted.

json_answer.flow_terminal_action: DirectNativeTransfer revert inside the refund callback. The attacker's contract either swallows it (the draw goes ahead) or it becomes a NativeRefundFailed revert of the whole requestDraw
json_answer.flow_security_relevance: requestDraw is the only raffle code that pushes native value to caller-controlled code, and it forwards all remaining gas. The receive() NatSpec also ties native intake to requestDraw. This flow shows that a bounced refund cannot be absorbed into the raffle balance and cannot change the half-written Drawing state. Its only effect is that the caller undoes its own draw request. requestDraw is permissionless, so anyone else can still request within the window.
